effects.log: You hold the lamp. It is a smaller honour and a truer one, and the steward afterward shows you the one lock kept back for the keeper of the cave.

events.text: On the wall behind {b3_anc} are painted every head of the house, in order, in plain strong lines, down to the last. There is blank wall under the last, and the paint, though old, is not dry. A brush lies on the ground. The steward says it dries by itself when the next head is chosen.

choices.text: Touch the paint, once

effects.log: It is wet under your fingertip, and warm, and when you draw back your finger there is nothing on it. You are not sure what you have done, and the house will say, later, that you were looked at.

choices.text: Look, and do not touch

effects.log: You look until your eyes ache. You do not touch. The steward, behind you, breathes out like someone who has been holding a long breath.

events.text: {b3_anc} comes down the swept path without any hurry, and the hall of {b3_house} empties around them like water from a basin. They stop in front of you, and look you over once from head to foot, the way one looks at a piece of furniture one has not seen moved. The first thing they say is "who let you sit there?"

choices.text: Answer: "the house did"

effects.log: You answer. The ancestor looks at the house, which looks at its feet, and a quiet falls in which it becomes plain the house did not.

choices.text: Answer: "nobody. I am sitting here because I can"

ok.log: The ancestor's mouth moves, not quite a smile. It is the first sign of interest in a very long time, and the house gasps.

fail.log: The answer rings false and arrogant, and the ancestor turns away as if you were a sound in another room.

events.text: {b3_anc} wakes, and for a long moment looks confused. Then they see the head's seat, and you in it, and all confusion goes. "I slept so that this house would not need me," they say, "and it has needed me four times since breakfast." The hall waits for a verdict.

choices.text: Say the house has done well without them

effects.log: You say so. They look at you for some time, and then, grudgingly, at the house, and the verdict is delayed, which is the best you could have hoped.

choices.text: Admit the house did need them

effects.log: You admit it, aloud. There is a low murmur of shock, and the ancestor gives a small dry laugh and says that is the first honest thing said in this hall since the war.

events.text: The ancestor {b3_anc} stands in the hall of {b3_house} and does not speak. The air is heavy with dust. The old head of the house, kneeling, whispers that the ancestor has not chosen a successor in nine hundred years and is not about to begin. The ancestor's eyes, across the hall, are on you.

choices.text: Kneel before the ancestor

effects.log: You kneel. The house gasps, not because you knelt but because the ancestor, for the first time in nine hundred years, has not made you.

choices.text: Remain standing, and meet the ancestor's eyes

effects.log: You remain standing. The silence stretches, and you hold, and it is the longest minute of your life.

events.text: Nobody has told {b3_anc} what year it is. The ancestor looks through a window at the garden and says that the great maple has grown. They ask how, then, did the house come to be led by someone with neither their name nor their face. It is a fair question, and asked in a most civil voice.

choices.text: Tell them the whole story, plainly

effects.log: You tell it plainly. It takes an hour, and the ancestor listens without a sound, and when you finish says it is a better story than they expected and a worse one than they feared.

choices.text: Say it is a long tale, and offer tea

effects.log: You offer tea. The ancestor, with a flicker of humour, accepts, and the tea is drunk in a silence that grows more companionable by the cup.

events.text: {b3_anc} puts a hand on the head's seat, the way one steadies a skittish animal. "This chair was made for someone who could lose," they say. "Can you?" The hall is rigid. A boy at the back, who cannot keep still, is the only one who breathes out.

choices.text: Say you have lost, many times

effects.log: You say so, and name three, and the ancestor, listening to the third, gives a tiny nod. It is not approval, but it is not the other thing either.

choices.text: Say you intend never to

effects.log: You say so. The ancestor stares at you for a long second and says that is a lie every head tells, and sits down to see how long you will keep telling it.

events.text: The ancestor {b3_anc} walks the length of the hall of {b3_house}, touching each pillar as if counting. At the fifth they stop, and say the pillar is wrong. It was carved with a different grain, once. The house is thunderstruck. The pillar was replaced six hundred years ago and no one living was told.

choices.text: Say the pillar was replaced, and why

effects.log: You tell them what the records say. The ancestor nods, slowly, and says the house kept its records, at least, and for the moment the hall breathes.

choices.text: Ask what the old pillar was like

effects.log: You ask. The ancestor describes it in a few worn words, and the house, listening, understands it has lost something it did not know it had.

events.text: A servant, terrified, spills tea at {b3_anc}'s feet. The hall freezes. The ancestor looks down at the tea, then at the servant, then at you, and raises one brow, and the servant goes the colour of paper. It is clear the head is expected to say something. Anything.

choices.text: Step forward and take the blame for the tea

effects.log: You take it. The ancestor looks at you for a very long time, and the servant is permitted to leave, and does, in a state of reverent shock.

choices.text: Order the servant to bring a cloth and fresh tea

effects.log: You order it, calmly. The ancestor's brow comes down; the servant bows and flees and returns, and the evening resumes.

events.text: The sleeper has woken with a headache. {b3_anc} sits on the steps of the great hall holding their temples and says that the house, in sleeping, has grown very loud. They ask for silence. The whole house, a thousand strong, tiptoes. You find yourself explaining the new chimney drum to an elder whose face you cannot read.

choices.text: Order the drum stopped for a week

effects.log: You stop it. The week is deathly quiet; the ancestor sleeps on the steps in sun like a cat, and the house, afterward, is a little less loud, ever after.

choices.text: Explain the drum, apologise, and offer a room by the garden

effects.log: You offer a room. The ancestor accepts at once, without thanks, and is never again seen on the steps.

events.text: {b3_anc} asks to see the accounts of {b3_house}. Not the summary: the accounts. The steward goes grey, brings them, and the ancestor reads in silence for an hour. When it is done they close the book. "You pay the cooks better than the tutors. Good. Tutors flatter. Cooks do not."

choices.text: Admit the tutors are paid too little

effects.log: You admit it. The ancestor has the grace to agree, and a decree is written the same hour, and the tutors, informed, do not quite know whom to thank.

choices.text: Say it was deliberate

effects.log: You say it was deliberate. The ancestor, to the house's surprise, laughs, and says the old head said the same, and meant it less.

events.text: The house sends children to greet {b3_anc}, hoping the sight of them will soften the ancestor. They line up, shuffling. The smallest steps out and offers the ancestor a half-eaten plum. The hall holds its breath. The ancestor accepts the plum, examines it, and eats.

choices.text: Let the child speak first

effects.log: The child says something about the plum that the entire hall will quote for a century. The ancestor is charmed, and your seat, for the day, is a little less hot.

choices.text: Step in, and thank the child for the house

effects.log: You step in and thank the child. The ancestor watches you do it, and says nothing, and on balance it is better than the alternative.

events.text: The ancestor {b3_anc} has, it seems, a favourite dish, and no one remembers it. The cooks bring forty plates, each wrong. After the fortieth the ancestor puts down their chopsticks and says, almost kindly, that it does not matter. Something in the hall breaks. The head cook is crying.

choices.text: Ask the ancestor to describe the dish

effects.log: You ask. The ancestor describes a soup, and the head cook, very old, says in a cracked voice that she has made that soup every winter on the ancestor's birthday for sixty years.

choices.text: Order the kitchen to bring the plain bowl of rice

effects.log: You order the rice. It is brought. The ancestor eats it in silence, and says it is exactly right, and nobody in the hall understands why.

events.text: You and {b3_anc} stand on the roof of {b3_house}, looking down on the courtyard. The ancestor says the house was built wrong, that the founder was a fool who loved a view. Then they say the house has also been loved wrong, for a long time, by people who did not look up.

choices.text: Say the house has learned to look up

effects.log: You say so. The ancestor does not turn, but the line of their shoulder softens, and you stay on the roof until the stars come out.

choices.text: Ask what they would change

effects.log: You ask. The ancestor gives you a list of twelve, from the gate to the kitchen, and you spend the following year doing eleven of them.

events.text: {b3_anc} stands before the shrine of the house and finds their own name on it. "Who put it there?" they ask. Nobody did; it has been there since the founding. The ancestor stares at it for a long time. Then they ask for a chisel, and the house, appalled, goes to find one.

choices.text: Hand them the chisel yourself

effects.log: You hand it over. The ancestor cuts the name away, slowly, and the stone beneath is bare, and the house is stricken, and the ancestor says now it is a shrine to something other than a dead name.

choices.text: Ask them not to; the house will cope

effects.log: You ask. The ancestor lowers the chisel and gives you a long, tired look, and the name stays, and you feel a coward and a diplomat in the same breath.

events.text: The ancestor and the old head of {b3_house} meet in the hall. They bow, correctly, and then, when they think nobody sees, grasp forearms and hold on, two very old people. The hall averts its eyes. You are the only one who notices that both are weeping.

choices.text: Give them the hall and clear the room

effects.log: You clear the room. The two sit all night in the empty hall. In the morning the old head hands you the seal, and says they were never so happy to be unseated.

choices.text: Stay in the corner and keep still

effects.log: You stay in the corner and keep still. When it is over the old head looks at you, and says nothing, and the nothing is a deep favour.

events.text: Before {b3_anc} will speak to anyone, they ask for a washbasin. It is brought. They wash their hands for a long time, in silence, and the whole hall watches, and when the water is grey they pour it out on the floor. A gift, whispers the steward, of the ancestor's own dust.

choices.text: Catch a little of the water in a cup

effects.log: You catch some. The steward pales; the ancestor, who sees, nods; and you have been, for a moment, the house's one person who did not flinch.

choices.text: Let it fall, and bow

effects.log: You let it fall and bow. The hall, relieved, bows with you, and a hundred knees creak, and the sound is that of a house deciding to forgive.

events.text: {npc} arrives with an aunt, a letter of terms, and a sealed box that has not been opened. The aunt sits very upright and does not drink. {npc} looks at you, then at the aunt, then at you again, with an expression so frank that the aunt coughs.

choices.text: Open with a question of your own, not a compliment

effects.log: You ask what {he} would be doing today if {he} were not here. {He} tells you, in detail, and the aunt stops pretending not to listen.

choices.text: Ask the aunt to step out for tea

effects.log: The aunt leaves with a bow of wonderful frost. When the door shuts {npc} laughs out loud, and the conversation begins.

events.text: {npc} has come on {his} own terms and has them written out. The letter of the match lists nine, from the habits of the household to what each shall say of the other at feasts. {He} has underlined the fifth: that neither will ever be asked to pretend to be someone they are not.

choices.text: Sign the fifth first, then read the rest

effects.log: You sign the fifth. {npc} looks at it a long moment, and then the other eight come one after another, all agreeable, and you wonder who is the cleverer of you.

choices.text: Propose a tenth term of your own

effects.log: You propose that each of you may leave for a month a year without explaining. {npc} considers it gravely, accepts, and adds an eleventh.

events.text: The match was arranged in your absence, and {npc} found out the same way you did: by being told. There is a moment in the receiving room in which each of you tries hard not to be the first to look relieved. {npc} says the arrangement is the most embarrassing thing that has ever happened to {him}.

choices.text: Agree that it is embarrassing, and laugh

effects.log: You laugh. {npc} laughs too, in a cracked, sudden way, and a relative in the next room tells another that it appears to be going well.

choices.text: Say it was not your idea, and not a bad one

effects.log: You say so. {npc} narrows {his} eyes and says that is possibly the most diplomatic sentence anyone has offered {him}.

events.text: {npc} is shown the gardens of your house and is polite about each and says nothing of any. At the last, a small plain pond, {he} stops. "This," {he} says, "is the only one made by a person who was not trying to be seen." It is a better compliment than you had any right to expect.

choices.text: Tell {him} who made it

effects.log: You tell {him}: your own hands, years ago, on a bad evening. {npc} nods gravely and says the match, whatever it is, has begun there.

choices.text: Say only that you are glad {he} likes it

effects.log: You say only that. {npc} smiles a small, particular smile, and the aunt, at a distance, starts to relax.

events.text: On the day, {npc} comes to the receiving room with a bandage on one hand. {He} says it was nothing. The aunt gives the full account: a stray cat, a tea service, an overturned shelf. {npc} studies the ceiling for all of it. The cat, you gather, now lives in {his} house.

choices.text: Ask after the cat

effects.log: You ask after the cat. {npc} brightens and tells you its name, its habits and its several betrayals, and the aunt gives up and pours the tea.

choices.text: Offer to rebind the hand

effects.log: You rebind it, badly, and {npc} says it is the best bandage {he} has ever had, because it is so plainly the work of a friend.

events.text: The house that offers {npc} wants something, as houses do. The aunt says only that {npc} has been raised to be a bridge, and that it is a hard thing to be. {npc} studies the floor. {He} does not look like a bridge. {He} looks like someone who would like to be asked.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what {he} wants, in front of the aunt

effects.log: You ask. The aunt stiffens; {npc} lifts {his} head and says what {he} wants in a few clear words, and it is nothing like what the house assumed.

choices.text: Talk terms with the aunt and let {npc} listen

effects.log: You talk terms. {npc} listens, and the aunt, turning at last, finds {him} watching you with an interest that has changed.

events.text: {npc} has brought a gift from {b3_house}, a small lacquered thing in a box within a box. {He} presents it with a bow that looks rehearsed. Inside is a spoon: a plain, old spoon. {npc} says it was the house's idea, that {he} does not know why, and that {he} has practised the bow for a week.

choices.text: Take the spoon and use it at once

effects.log: You stir the tea with it. {npc} stares, the aunt chokes, and it turns out the spoon is a blessing of the house meant to be used. {npc} lets out a breath.

choices.text: Admire it and set it on the shelf of honour

effects.log: You set it on the shelf. It looks lonely and exactly right, and {npc} looks at it, at the shelf, and at you, and smiles.

events.text: {npc} is nine hundred years older than the match makes either of you look, and has the manners of it. {He} sits as if the cushion were an honour guard. {He} says {he} has outlived two spouses and the trick was never to be surprised. Then {he} looks at you, and is visibly surprised.

choices.text: Ask what surprised {him}

effects.log: {npc} says: that you had asked. Nobody has asked in four hundred years, and the conversation runs on till the lamps burn low.

choices.text: Say you hope to go on surprising for a long while

effects.log: You say so. {npc} lifts a brow and a corner of the mouth, and the aunt, taking in the tableau, bows low and withdraws.

events.text: You and {npc} have been left alone in the library by arrangement, and both of you know it. The silence is of the kind that is full of other people listening. {npc} picks up a book and reads a page aloud, deadpan: a recipe for dumplings. Behind the screen, someone cannot hold it, and sneezes.

choices.text: Read the next page back, in the same voice

effects.log: You read on. It is a treatise on drains. The screen shakes, {npc} sinks into a chair, and the match, it appears, will go ahead.

choices.text: Tell {him} the sneezer is your own cousin

effects.log: You tell {him}. {npc} says the one on {his} side is an uncle, and for the first time the pair of you are allies.

events.text: {npc} reminds you of someone you half-loved in a century long past. It is not the face, which is quite different; it is the way {he} pours tea. You find you are staring, and stop. {npc} says that on the matter of the pouring, {he} has been told before.

choices.text: Tell {him} who it reminds you of

effects.log: You tell {him} the whole old story. {npc} listens, then says quietly that {he} has one of those too, and between the two stories the first honest hour begins.

choices.text: Say it is only the light

effects.log: You say it is only the light. {npc} gives you a look that says {he} does not believe it, and lets it go with grace.

events.text: A rumour reaches {npc} that you have a temper. It reaches you that {npc} bites. You each arrive prepared, and sit rigid and ceremonious, glaring at the tea. Then {npc} says from behind the cup that {he} has never bitten anyone in {his} life and wishes {he} had the nerve.

choices.text: Say you have no temper, but would like to try one

effects.log: You say it. {npc} chokes on the tea, the aunt arrives with a cloth, and the pair of you cannot be separated for the afternoon.

choices.text: Admit the temper is real, and describe its worst day

effects.log: You describe it. {npc} nods with a professional gravity and says that was a very useful hour, and takes notes.

events.text: The match comes with an escort: eleven people in the house colours, each carrying a tray, arranged along the wall like decorative birds. {npc} apologises. {He} asked for three, and the house felt the gap was a statement. The eleven take a step in unison, to prove they are three.

choices.text: Greet each tray-bearer by name

effects.log: You greet them, every one, from a quietly memorised list. The eleven are amazed and pleased, and {npc} watches you with new and cautious respect.

choices.text: Send the eleven to the kitchen for a meal

effects.log: You send them. They go, delighted, and {npc} and you have your first quiet hour to the sound of a distant feast.

events.text: {npc} asks you outright whether you want this. The aunt is not in the room, which means {he} has contrived that the aunt should not be. "I will say yes if you do," {he} says. "I will say no if you do. But I want to know before I go to the house, because I know what they will want me to say."

choices.text: Say yes, and mean it

effects.log: You say yes. {npc} looks at you, long, and says yes back, and the matter begins with a plainness that startles the pair of you.

choices.text: Say you are not sure, and would like to find out

effects.log: You say so. {npc} lets out a breath held a long time, says that is the best answer, and you spend the next year finding out.

events.text: The terms of the match are read aloud in the receiving room by a very old herald. They include precedence at feasts, the number of lamps, the wording of a toast, and a clause concerning the care of a certain heirloom screen. {npc} has been trying not to catch your eye. At the clause on the screen, {he} fails.

choices.text: Return the look, deadpan

effects.log: You return it. {npc} collapses behind a sleeve, the herald loses the place and begins the clause again, louder, to the bewildered delight of the room.

choices.text: Keep a very serious face for the herald

effects.log: You keep it. The herald finishes with a flourish, and afterwards {npc} says you deserve a medal for that, and presents you with a plum.

events.text: It emerges that {npc} and you share a great-great-grandmother. This is not unusual in old houses; it is why aunts check. The aunt checks again in front of you, with a long list, and at the end says the relation is thin enough, and sits back like a judge.

choices.text: Say the family is just very small

effects.log: You say so. {npc} laughs, the aunt frowns very slightly, and the match goes on, sealed by a joke.

choices.text: Ask to see the list yourself

effects.log: You read the list. It is exhaustive. On the fourth line you find a mistake, and the aunt, scandalised and thrilled, thanks you with a deep bow.

events.text: {npc}'s house requires the match to climb the hundred steps to its gate on foot, carrying the betrothal gift unaided. The gift weighs about as much as a small calf. {npc}, at the top, watches you labour with the look of someone who did the same last year and is delighted not to be alone.

choices.text: Make it to the top and set the gift down gently

effects.log: You make it, and set it down. {npc} claps once and says the climb is the real betrothal and the rest is paperwork.

choices.text: Stop halfway and ask {npc} to come down and share it

effects.log: {npc} comes down, takes the other end, and you reach the top together, which the house frowns upon and the servants adore.

events.text: {npc} is better at the board game than you, and better at the game of the match, and is open about both. {He} says so with such delight at your being a worthy opponent that offence is impossible. After the third game, won by a single stone, {he} says you are the first to make it close.

choices.text: Ask for a rematch

effects.log: You ask. {npc} grins and accepts, and the house, passing, hears the click of stones until dawn.

choices.text: Praise the single stone

effects.log: You say the single stone was elegant. {npc} flushes, pleased and shy, and the aunt, at the door, finally picks up the tea.

events.text: A rival suitor of the same house arrives unannounced, with flowers and a carriage. {npc} had not mentioned a rival. The suitor, smooth and handsome, stands in the middle of the receiving room and begins a speech about the antiquity of their line. {npc} looks, with deep composure, at the ceiling.

choices.text: Let the suitor finish, then ask one question

effects.log: You ask what the suitor likes to do on a wet afternoon. The suitor founders. {npc} turns to you, eyes bright, and the speech is quietly abandoned.

choices.text: Send for tea, and a second chair for the suitor

effects.log: You send for them. The suitor, thrown by the hospitality, leaves early, and {npc} takes your arm for the first time, on the veranda.

events.text: You were told that {npc} dislikes music, and the musicians were dismissed. Then {npc} arrives and asks, delicately, why there is none. A bad flautist at some other function put the rumour about. {npc} loves music, plays three instruments, and has brought one in a case.

choices.text: Ask {him} to play

effects.log: {npc} plays. It is strange and tender and badly out of practice, and the room tilts toward {him} like a field in wind.

choices.text: Recall the musicians, and take a drum yourself

effects.log: The result is chaos and joy, and {npc} says through the noise that this is the loudest match in the history of the house.

events.text: In the records of {b3_house}, where the match is entered, there is a blank line: the line for what you bring. {npc} says the aunts debate it each time, and the entries are always modest and false. {He} suggests, with the faintest smile, that you write something true and see what the aunts make of it.

choices.text: Write "a poor sense of direction and a good ear"

effects.log: You write it. The aunts are bewildered; the oldest says it is the only honest entry in six hundred years, and files it with a small ceremony.

choices.text: Write only your name

effects.log: You write your name. {npc} reads it thoughtfully and says it is the best line in the book.

events.text: {npc} has a habit of falling silent mid-sentence and resuming as if no gap had occurred. At first you think it is nerves. Then you notice it happens when {he} is looking at something far away. {He} admits, embarrassed, that {he} has been listening for the voice of {his} own house, and cannot find it.

choices.text: Tell {him} you will listen with {him}

effects.log: You sit with {him} and listen. After a while a very faint sound comes, which may be wind or may not, and {npc} turns to you with wet eyes.

choices.text: Say the house is not worth the listening

effects.log: You say so. {npc} stares, shocked, then laughs for a full minute, and does not stop being fond for years.

events.text: At the feast that follows the match, {npc} sits beside you with a blank dish before {him}. {He} whispers that the cook is {his} oldest friend and has made the dish {he} loved as a child. It arrives. It is plain porridge. {npc} eats every spoonful and says it is the best meal of {his} life.

choices.text: Ask for a bowl of the same

effects.log: It is brought. The porridge is excellent, and the cook watches two grown immortals eat it with a quiet joy that makes you resolve to do something for the cook.

choices.text: Compliment the cook by name to the room

effects.log: You do. The room is surprised, and the cook disappears into the kitchen and is heard to cry.

events.text: The night before the match is sealed, {npc} sends you a note by a child. It says: "I snore." Nothing else. You are left to decide what a person means by telling you that, the night before. In the morning {npc} is at the gate, rigid, waiting to see what your face does.

choices.text: Send the child back with "so do I"

effects.log: The child runs back with it. At the gate {npc} breaks into a helpless grin, and the whole matter, after that, is easy.

choices.text: Greet {him} with a nod and say nothing of it

effects.log: You nod. {npc} studies your face for a long second and relaxes, and over the years the snoring is never once mentioned, and always known.

events.text: Your matchmaker, an ancient and formidable woman, has a ledger of every match in the history of the house, with notes on how each turned out. She turns to yours and reads: "Likely to quarrel about the lamps. Likely to forgive by morning." She closes the book with a snap. "Do not tell them I said so."

choices.text: Ask what the matchmaker wrote about {npc}

effects.log: She tells you, reluctantly, one line, and it is such a kind line that you keep it for a century.

choices.text: Ask her to write the next line when the lamps are decided

effects.log: She snorts, and writes it in at once, in a hand so small you have to hold it to the light.

events.text: The cook of {b3_clan} is past eighty and has burned the rice three mornings running. Nobody dares say so. The children eat it anyway, with the faces of martyrs. {b3_elder} takes you aside and says the cook has fed four heads of the house and is owed something better than a quiet word.

choices.text: Name a successor and keep the cook as adviser

effects.log: You name a young apprentice and keep the old cook at the stove-side as adviser. The old cook grumbles for a month and then sits there like a queen.

choices.text: Ask the cook outright to step aside

effects.log: You ask outright. The cook goes very still, then agrees, and the kitchen is silent for a week as if in mourning.

events.text: The new cook of {b3_clan} makes a lighter, stranger soup, and half the house will not eat it. The old cook, in the corner, has not said a word. Then at the feast the old cook rises, tastes the new soup in front of everyone, and puts down the spoon.

choices.text: Ask the old cook for a plain verdict

effects.log: You ask. The old cook says it is very good, and a little too clever, and needs more salt, which is the exact right thing, and the house exhales.

choices.text: Change the subject and call for the music

effects.log: You call for the music. The moment passes, and the soup is quietly improved over the next month without anyone admitting why.

events.text: Many years on, the old cook of {b3_clan} is on a pallet by the stove, very small, with a bowl of the new soup. The household has gathered in the kitchen without being told. The old cook says that the rice was never burned. It was the only way to get you to come down to the kitchen.

choices.text: Sit by the pallet through the night

effects.log: You sit through the night. By morning the old cook is gone, and the new cook has put a bowl of burned rice at the head of the table, and nobody touches it.

choices.text: Promise the kitchen will be kept as it is

effects.log: You promise. The old cook smiles, shuts both eyes, and the promise is kept, and the kitchen is, to this day, the warmest room in the house.

events.text: Two branches of {b3_clan} have been feuding for a century over a boundary pond. It has no fish and no beauty. You are asked to arbitrate. {b3_elder} says the pond is only a story they tell to avoid saying the thing underneath. Each branch brings a delegation of cousins in matching sashes.

choices.text: Drain the pond in front of both branches

effects.log: You have the pond drained. Underneath is a child's toy boat, rotted but whole, and both branches go quiet, and then, to your astonishment, together, they cry.

choices.text: Rule that the pond belongs to the house, not to either branch

effects.log: You rule so. Both branches are furious, and united in it, which is, in a way, the first agreement in a century.

events.text: An envoy from a rival house arrives at {b3_clan} dressed all in white, which at this season means a wedding is offered or a funeral is demanded. The envoy keeps the secret with irritating gaiety. {b3_peer} has already prepared both responses and will not say which.

choices.text: Receive the envoy as for a wedding

effects.log: It is a wedding. The envoy bursts into relieved laughter, and an alliance of two houses is begun over very good plum wine.

choices.text: Receive the envoy as for a death

effects.log: You receive the envoy as for a death. It is a death, and you have been gracious in the one hour in which it counted, and the other house does not forget.

events.text: The house tutor of {b3_clan} resigns in a letter written in a very fine hand and five pages long. The first page is grievances. The fifth is a recommendation of the best pupil the house has ever had, a quiet girl whom nobody had noticed. {b3_elder} says the tutor was right about everything.

choices.text: Give the quiet child the tutor's own library

effects.log: You give her the library. She reads it all in two years, and then starts to correct the footnotes.

choices.text: Hire a famous replacement and keep the child in the class

effects.log: You hire a famous scholar. The child sits in the back row, learning more from watching the scholar be wrong than from anything he says.

events.text: A cousin of {b3_clan} has fallen in love with someone from a house that is, officially, an enemy. The cousin comes to you at night, in tears and a very good robe. The enemy house, it turns out, has a cousin who has done the same thing. They have been meeting at the shrine.

choices.text: Arrange a feast to which both are invited

effects.log: You arrange it. The two houses, seated at one table, take a very long hour to speak, and then speak for six.

choices.text: Keep the secret and let the two meet quietly

effects.log: You keep the secret. The two meet at the shrine for a year, and the thing grows beyond what either house can now stop.

events.text: The ancestral the cloud tablets of {b3_clan} have been wiped by a leak in the roof. Half the names are gone. {b3_elder} says the names can be recovered from the register, and the register, it turns out, is also leaking. What the house has left is the memory of its oldest servants.

choices.text: Gather the old servants and have them dictate

effects.log: You gather them. They dictate for three days, arguing, and the names come back, and a few of them, to everyone's delight, are different from what the house remembered.

choices.text: Rewrite them from the register and leave the gaps

effects.log: You rewrite from the register and leave the gaps, plainly marked. It is an honest board, and it draws more visitors than the old one.

events.text: A merchant offers {b3_clan} an unreasonable sum for the old orchard, which grows nothing of value. {b3_peer} says the merchant knows something. {b3_elder} says the orchard is the house. A child, listening, says the merchant is not a merchant at all, but has the wrong hands.

choices.text: Refuse, and have the stranger followed

effects.log: You refuse and have him followed. He turns out to be a scholar of a faraway house who believes the orchard stands on a buried library.

choices.text: Accept the offer, with conditions

effects.log: You accept with conditions, and the stranger meets them all, and the orchard is cleared, and under the roots is a small stone door.

events.text: The house gate of {b3_clan} has a hinge that sings. It has sung for sixty years and the house has stopped hearing it. A visiting guest remarks on it at dinner. Overnight, every servant in the house gets up and oils it. In the morning the house wakes to a silence so complete that no one can sleep.

choices.text: Have the hinge un-oiled

effects.log: You have it un-oiled. The singing returns, and the house sleeps better than it has in a decade.

choices.text: Keep the silence and see how the house adjusts

effects.log: You keep it. It takes the house a month to learn the new quiet, and a year to stop checking whether the gate is still there.

events.text: It is the season for the house's great the Moon Feast, and the steward of {b3_clan} has made an error in the guest list: two houses that must not be seated together are seated together. The error is discovered an hour before dinner. {b3_peer} suggests a small fire as a distraction, and is told to stop being helpful.

choices.text: Seat them at opposite ends and say it is the custom

effects.log: You seat them far apart and claim it is the custom. By the third course each house has decided the other is the wiser for adhering to it.

choices.text: Go to each guest and confess the mistake

effects.log: You confess to each in turn. Both are so disarmed by the honesty that they spend the dinner outdoing each other in graciousness.

events.text: A traveller is found asleep in the gatehouse of {b3_clan}, in a coat that clearly belonged to someone grander. {b3_elder} says to turn the stranger out. {b3_peer} says to feed them. The stranger wakes and says, perfectly politely, that the coat is stolen and would you like it back.

choices.text: Take the coat back and feed the stranger

effects.log: You take the coat and give the stranger breakfast. They eat like a wolf and leave before noon with a bundle and a blessing.

choices.text: Let the stranger keep the coat and go

effects.log: You let them keep it. A year later a letter arrives from a distant house, thanking you in terms so odd you cannot tell if it is sincere.

events.text: A scholar comes to {b3_clan} to write its history and is horrified by the state of the archive. The scholar stays two months. At the end, the scholar says the house has been wrong about its own founding. The founder was not a hero; the founder was a very clever woman who ran a laundry.

choices.text: Publish the true history in the house chronicle

effects.log: You publish it. Half the house is dismayed, and half is delighted, and the laundry becomes a shrine.

choices.text: Keep it in the archive, to be read by heads only

effects.log: You keep it in the archive. Each new head reads it once, and weeps, and laughs, and tells nobody.

events.text: A fire in the east wing of {b3_clan} burns for an hour before it is put out. No one is hurt. The east wing is the oldest. What remains is a blackened frame, a smell of old cedar, and a cat sitting in the ashes looking offended. {b3_elder} says the wing will cost a fortune to rebuild.

choices.text: Rebuild exactly as it was

effects.log: You rebuild it exactly. It takes three years and drains the house, and the east wing, when finished, looks as though it had never burned, which is its own kind of lie.

choices.text: Rebuild it differently, with a courtyard open to the sky

effects.log: You rebuild it with a courtyard. The old ones grumble; the young ones sit in it at dusk, and the cat claims it.

events.text: The young heir of {b3_clan} announces at breakfast that they will not take the seat. They would rather be a painter. The table goes silent. {b3_elder} drops a spoon. The heir, trembling, looks only at you.

choices.text: Let the heir paint, and name another successor

effects.log: You let the heir paint. The house is shocked, then resigned, and the heir's first painting, hung in the hall, is a portrait of you that no one dares mock.

choices.text: Ask the heir to try the seat for a year first

effects.log: You ask for a year. The heir agrees, miserable, and at the year's end both of you know the answer, and are kinder to each other for having waited.

events.text: A spirit of the hearth has settled in {b3_clan}, unasked. It breaks nothing, steals nothing, and every morning rearranges the shoes at the door into a neat row. The servants leave it milk. {b3_peer} says it must be exorcised. {b3_elder} says it is the best-behaved resident the house has had.

choices.text: Leave it be, and leave out a saucer

effects.log: You leave it be. The shoes are tidier ever after, and the house acquires a quiet reputation for good luck.

choices.text: Ask the spirit what it wants

effects.log: You ask, aloud, to the empty hall. The next morning every shoe in the house is turned to face the door, which you take to mean it wants to be asked again.

events.text: The yearly accounts of {b3_clan} show a small, neat discrepancy in the kitchen budget, the same size every year for twenty years. Nobody has noticed because the amount is so exactly an apple. {b3_peer} suspects theft. {b3_elder} suspects a very old kindness.

choices.text: Follow the apple

effects.log: You follow it. Every year, one apple goes to an old woman in the lane, who was once a servant of the house, and has no one. You say nothing, and double the apple.

choices.text: Let the apple be, and mention it to no one

effects.log: You let it be. It is the quietest charity the house has, and you resolve to deserve it.

events.text: The house of {b3_clan} is asked by the Jade Court to send a dozen of its young to serve a term in the capital. It is an honour and a hostage-taking, and everyone knows both. The young want to go. The old do not want them to. {b3_peer} offers to go in their place, to everyone's surprise.

choices.text: Send the young, with {b3_peer} as their keeper

effects.log: You send them. The twelve return in three years, polished, wary and in debt to a dozen people, and the house is a little taller than before.

choices.text: Refuse politely and send gifts instead

effects.log: You refuse. The court frowns, and the gifts are accepted with a long silence, and the matter is not forgotten.

events.text: Two sisters of {b3_clan} stop speaking over a ring. It was their mother's. Neither wanted it for the ring. Each says the other took the last word the mother spoke, which neither will repeat. The house has gone cold at both ends. {b3_elder} says it will be a decade.

choices.text: Put the two in a room with the ring and lock the door

effects.log: You lock them in. At dawn they come out arm in arm, red-eyed, and the ring is on neither of their hands; it is on yours.

choices.text: Give the ring to the house shrine, and say nothing

effects.log: You give it to the shrine. The sisters are silent, and then, in the spring, share a bench at the festival, and neither mentions it.

events.text: A young man comes to {b3_clan} to say he is the head's long-lost cousin, and he has a letter, and a crest, and a nose exactly like the founder's. The nose is the problem; it is all too perfect. {b3_peer} says he is a fraud. {b3_elder} says the nose, however, is real.

choices.text: Admit him as a guest and watch him

effects.log: You admit him. He is a fraud, and an amiable one, and he turns out to know more of the house's history than the house.

choices.text: Send him away with a night's lodging

effects.log: You send him off with a bed and breakfast. A year later you hear that he has set up as a genealogist, and is very good.

events.text: There is a tree in the courtyard of {b3_clan} that has never flowered. The house has cut it down thrice and it has grown back. This spring, it blooms, in one night, white, everywhere, in the wrong season. The house stands at the windows, silent. {b3_elder} says no one living has seen it.

choices.text: Hold a vigil under the tree

effects.log: You hold a vigil. By dawn the blossoms have fallen, and the house is covered in petals, and every child in it is given a petal to keep.

choices.text: Have the blossoms painted and recorded

effects.log: You have them painted. The scroll hangs in the hall, and is looked at by every guest, and the tree, never again, flowers.

events.text: The head of a rival house dies, and {b3_clan} is expected to send a delegation of mourning. {b3_peer} says the dead head was a snake. {b3_elder} says the dead head was also an old friend, once, and a better one than either of you has had.

choices.text: Go yourself, and speak at the mourning

effects.log: You go. You speak plainly of what the dead was, snake and friend. The rival house, expecting a lie, hears something better, and sends a gift of thanks.

choices.text: Send a wreath and a graceful note

effects.log: You send them. The note is perfect, and unremarked, and the rival house files it with the others.

events.text: A well in the yard of {b3_clan} has gone dry after a thousand seasons. The old well-keeper insists it is a sign. The young engineer insists it is a water table. Both of them follow you around for a week, each arguing, in turn, behind the other's back.

choices.text: Dig deeper, and ask the keeper to bless the new bore

effects.log: You do both. Water comes at forty feet, sweet and cold, and keeper and engineer share the credit and a secret contempt.

choices.text: Close the well and tell the house to use the river

effects.log: You close it. The house walks to the river every morning, and talks more on the way than it ever did at the well.

events.text: An envoy from the Jade Court arrives to inspect {b3_clan}, and the house polishes for a week. The inspector finds a piece of dust in the exact centre of the great table, which has plainly been left there with the greatest care. The inspector says nothing, and writes a report that is entirely a poem.

choices.text: Frame the poem and hang it in the hall

effects.log: You frame it. The inspector, hearing, sends a case of wine, and the house acquires the mild fame of having been a subject of art.

choices.text: Have the dust swept, and the poem kept in a drawer

effects.log: You sweep and keep. The drawer fills over the years, with other things left by other guests, and you realise the house has become an archive of small kindnesses.

events.text: A child of {b3_clan} asks you why the house has so many rules. You start to answer and find you cannot. {b3_elder} listens at the door. You promise to find out, and spend a month asking every old person in the house the reason for one rule each. Nobody can say. Several make up very good answers.

choices.text: Publish the rules with the made-up reasons beside them

effects.log: You publish the whole compendium. It is the funniest document in the archive, and the house follows its rules more carefully out of sheer affection.

choices.text: Strike out the ones nobody can explain

effects.log: You strike out nineteen. The house is astonished to find it carries on very well without them, and the child checks the list every year.

events.text: A young woman of {b3_clan} has been spotted three nights running on the roof, singing in a language no one knows. She says she is not singing; she is answering. {b3_elder} says she should be confined. {b3_peer} says she should be listened to, at a safe distance.

choices.text: Go up on the roof and listen

effects.log: You go up. The song is strange and slow, and by the third verse you understand a few words, and by the fourth you wish you did not.

choices.text: Ask her what she is answering

effects.log: She tells you: a voice from under the house. It has been asking something for a century and no one has answered it. She says it is only asking whether the lamps are lit.

events.text: On the anniversary of the founding the house of {b3_clan} sings its anthem, which nobody can sing. It has seven verses and a key change in the middle. The choir, this year, has grown ambitious, and sets out to do all seven. At the key change, a cat walks into the hall.

choices.text: Let the cat conduct

effects.log: You let the cat conduct. It walks the length of the hall, tail up, and the choir follows, in perfect tune, to the end. The cat is given the first plate.

choices.text: Stop the choir at the key change and ask for the last verse alone

effects.log: You ask for the last verse. It is sung by a small boy at the back, in a voice like water, and the hall wipes its eyes.

events.text: A grandson of {b3_clan} has been missing three days. The house searches. On the fourth day the boy is found at the top of the bell tower, with a stolen cake, a book, and a lantern, in a nest he built himself. He says he is on a retreat. {b3_elder} says he is the first of the house to find a use for the tower.

choices.text: Give the boy the tower as a study

effects.log: You give it. He reads there for twenty years and becomes the house's best historian.

choices.text: Bring him down and feed him, then ask what he read

effects.log: You bring him down. He tells you about the book, at length, in a rush, and you realise it is the same one you hid up there when you were young.

events.text: Every year {b3_clan} must send tribute to the Jade Court, and every year the amount is questioned. This year the collector is new and honest, and has found a discrepancy in the house's favour. The collector says a mistake of that size has to be reported. The mistake, if reported, will ruin an old accountant.

choices.text: Pay the difference quietly, and ask the collector to forget it

effects.log: You pay the difference. The collector looks at you for a while and says honesty is a short-lived trade, and takes it, and goes.

choices.text: Let the collector report it and stand by the accountant

effects.log: You stand by the accountant. The report is made, the penalty paid, the accountant retires with honour, and the house is thought, in some circles, to have a spine.

events.text: The oldest tutor of {b3_clan} asks, before dying, to be buried with the house's children. Not in the family ground; in the schoolroom, under the floor. It has been done once before, in a house nobody remembers. The elders recoil. The children, told, ask if they can paint the floor.

choices.text: Allow it, and let the children paint

effects.log: You allow it. The floor is painted with a river and eleven ducks, and the tutor rests beneath, and the schoolroom is the best-attended room in the house.

choices.text: Bury the tutor in the family ground, and carve the tutor's name over the schoolroom door

effects.log: You bury and carve. The elders approve; the children grumble; the name over the door is touched by every child entering for a century.

events.text: A monk comes to {b3_clan} in a storm, soaked, and asks for a room for the night. At dinner the monk eats nothing but rice and says nothing at all. In the morning the house finds that every lamp has been trimmed, every shoe straightened, every cup turned. The monk is gone.

choices.text: Set a place for the monk at the next dinner

effects.log: You set a place. Nobody comes, and the house eats with the empty chair, and the custom stays, and no one dares break it.

choices.text: Look for the monk on the road

effects.log: You send out riders. They find nothing, but a boy at the crossroads says that a monk gave him a coin and asked him to give the house its thanks.

events.text: The boundary stone between {b3_clan} and a neighbour has moved six inches in the night. Nobody has touched it. Both houses blame the other. Both send riders. On the second morning it moves again, another six inches, toward the neighbour. The neighbour stops complaining and starts to look pale.

choices.text: Watch the stone one night yourself

effects.log: You sit by it all night. At dawn it moves, slowly, by itself, and you see, beneath, the tip of a root growing toward the neighbour's well.

choices.text: Propose to the neighbour that the stone be allowed to wander

effects.log: You propose it. The neighbour agrees, with relief. The stone goes on wandering for a hundred years, and neither house ever says it is theirs.

events.text: A letter reaches {b3_clan} every spring from the head of a rival house, unsigned, written in a beautiful hand, and containing only a single sentence of insult. This year the insult is clever. {b3_elder} confesses to having looked forward to it all winter.

choices.text: Answer in kind, with a better insult

effects.log: You write a better one. The reply, next spring, is better still, and a correspondence of high art is begun.

choices.text: Answer with a sincere compliment

effects.log: You write that the hand is the finest you have seen. The next spring brings a blank page, which you frame.

events.text: The rival's letter this spring is not an insult. It is four lines of verse about a death in their house. They have signed it. {b3_peer} says it is a trap. {b3_elder} sits for a long time with it before saying it is the first honest thing the rival has written in thirty years.

choices.text: Go in person to the rival's house

effects.log: You go. The rival, old and thin, receives you at the gate in plain clothes, and the two of you drink tea in a silence as much a feast as any you have attended.

choices.text: Send an answer in verse, and a gift of the same weight

effects.log: You send verse and gift. The rival writes no more insults, but a good deal more verse.

events.text: The rival's heir comes to {b3_clan} with a satchel of letters, thirty years of them, all the insults kept. The rival has died. The satchel is the only inheritance they left, with a note: "Burn if you wish. Read first." The heir waits for you to decide.

choices.text: Read them all, with the heir, over a long evening

effects.log: You read them all. Thirty years of insults turn out to be thirty years of love, in disguise, and the heir weeps, and you do not blame them.

choices.text: Burn them, ceremonially, in the courtyard

effects.log: You burn them. The smoke goes up straight, and the heir bows to it, and both houses, from that day, are one in all but name.

events.text: An old retainer of {b3_clan} stops one night at your door and asks if she can be released from service. She is a hundred and four. Nobody has ever asked. The household law has no clause for it. {b3_elder} looks at the ceiling. She wants to see the sea, she says, before the next season.

choices.text: Release her with a pension and a travelling companion

effects.log: You release her. She sees the sea, and sends the house a single shell, which hangs now in the great hall, and stays there.

choices.text: Ask her to stay one more season, and then go together to the sea

effects.log: You go with her at the end of the season. She stands in the surf and does not say a word, and you remember it.

events.text: The treasury-keeper of {b3_clan} reports that someone has been taking small things from the family vault and leaving small things in return: a comb, a cup, a carved fish. The exchange is always, by weight, slightly in the house's favour. The keeper is not sure whether to feel robbed.

choices.text: Set a watch on the vault

effects.log: You set a watch. The thief turns out to be a small child, very serious, running a private trade with a spirit that lives in the wall.

choices.text: Leave something out for the thief on purpose

effects.log: You leave a small jar of honey. It is gone by morning, and in its place is a stone shaped like a heart, and you carry it for years.

events.text: Your cousin keeps a menagerie in a wing of {b3_clan}: twenty-two creatures from eleven worlds, none of them quite legal. A visiting official sniffs and asks to see the permits. The cousin turns the colour of old paper. A peacock lets out a shriek.

choices.text: Declare the menagerie a ward of the house

effects.log: You declare it. The official, outwitted, writes it up, and the cousin loves you for a decade.

choices.text: Hold a "tour" for the official and let the creatures speak for themselves

effects.log: You hold a tour. The peacock sits on the official's shoulder, a toad eats the report, and the official leaves laughing helplessly and does not come back.

events.text: A drought has dried the lands under {b3_clan}. The tenants come to the gate in silence. {b3_peer} points out that the cloud larder holds enough to feed the house for two years, or the tenants for one. {b3_elder} does not speak, which in a person of that temper is a statement.

choices.text: Open the cloud larder to the tenants

effects.log: You open it. The house is thinner for two years, and the tenants, for a century, tell the story at every wedding.

choices.text: Open it by half and send riders for help

effects.log: You open half. The riders return with help, late, and the compromise leaves no one satisfied, and everyone alive.

events.text: The ceiling of the great hall of {b3_clan} is painted with the founders, nine of them, in a ring. One has been scrubbed out. Nobody knows when. A shape remains, a pale outline, a figure whose head is turned. {b3_elder} says it is deliberate. {b3_peer} says it is damp.

choices.text: Have a painter restore the missing founder from the archive

effects.log: You hire a painter. The archive has nothing, so the painter makes the face from a dozen descendants. The founder, when finished, looks uncannily like you.

choices.text: Leave the outline, and add a placard: "unknown"

effects.log: You leave it. The outline becomes the most discussed thing in the house, and a place children go to dare each other.

events.text: A rumour spreads that {b3_clan} has a secret treasure. It is not true. Treasure-hunters begin to arrive, each with a map. The maps are all different. {b3_peer} delights in showing them the archive, where the real secret is that the house has never had a map of itself.

choices.text: Sell the visitors tea and a tour

effects.log: You sell tea and a tour. The house prospers modestly, and the treasure-hunters go away with a story and a cold.

choices.text: Make a treasure and bury it for them

effects.log: You bury a small chest in the orchard. It is found within the week by a hunter who weeps over its contents: a child's drawings of the house, one per head, going back centuries.

events.text: The isle bell of {b3_clan} cracked in the night. It has rung every hour for two hundred years. Now it makes a sound like a goose. The whole house is waking at the wrong time, apologising to each other. A bellfounder arrives, grim, with a quote that makes {b3_elder} sit down.

choices.text: Pay for the recast

effects.log: You pay. The new bell has a clean, brash note, and the house takes a year to forgive it.

choices.text: Keep the cracked bell, and let it honk

effects.log: You keep it. The goose-bell becomes the house's emblem, and the neighbours grow to love it and set their days by its honk.

events.text: A pair of twin cousins of {b3_clan} are exactly alike and have always been mistaken for each other. This year they decide to swap lives for a month, as a game, and tell no one. The house plays along. It becomes unclear after a week which twin is which, and the twins themselves begin to lose track.

choices.text: Call the twins to the hall and ask each to name the other

effects.log: You ask. Each names the other correctly, with some effort, and cries. Both are somewhat shaken, and the game is called off.

choices.text: Let the game run its month

effects.log: You let it run. At the end of the month the twins are two different people, finally, and prefer it that way.

events.text: The chief steward of {b3_clan} has served for sixty years and has never taken a day off. He asks, in a trembling voice, for one afternoon, to attend a performance in the lane. He has never seen a play. His assistant says the house will fall without him. The house, you think, will manage a Thursday.

choices.text: Give him the afternoon, and go with him

effects.log: You go. The play is dreadful and he weeps through all of it, and thanks you, in the lane after, with a stiff little bow you remember always.

choices.text: Give him a month's leave, with a stipend

effects.log: You give him the month. He spends it at plays, and comes back transformed, and is, for a decade, the most theatrical steward on record.

events.text: A famous painter is invited to {b3_clan} to do the portrait of the head of the house. The painter stares at you for an hour and puts down the brush. "I cannot," the painter says. "You are not what you look like." The painter will not elaborate. The house is rattled.

choices.text: Ask the painter what, then, you are

effects.log: The painter says: someone listening to a sound that has not happened yet. You think about it for a decade.

choices.text: Send the painter away with a gift and no portrait

effects.log: You send the painter off with silk. In the hall, there is a blank space where the portrait would be, and the house becomes fond of it.

events.text: The children of {b3_clan} have found the roof of the great hall and made a world on it: a village of twigs, a river of spilled tea, a war between two clans of snails. They invite you, as an honoured guest, to adjudicate a border dispute. The snails' side is represented by a very small girl with a stick.

choices.text: Adjudicate with great seriousness

effects.log: You rule for the snails in a long solemn judgment. The girl is satisfied beyond measure, and the borders hold for years.

choices.text: Propose a treaty with a shared tea-river

effects.log: You propose it. The children accept, awed, and the treaty is written on a leaf and kept in the archive as a primary source.

events.text: The yearly gathering of the many branches of {b3_clan} descends on the house, six hundred relatives, all talking. Every year a cousin claims to be wronged, and every year it is a different cousin. This year the cousin is young, and furious, and right.

choices.text: Hear the cousin out in front of everyone, and concede

effects.log: You hear them and concede. The six hundred are silent, and then a low, uneasy applause begins, which nobody has ever heard in that hall.

choices.text: Hear the cousin in private and settle it quietly

effects.log: You settle it quietly. The cousin is satisfied, and the hall is not scandalised, and nothing is changed except that a small wrong is no longer there.

events.text: The aunt of {b3_clan} who has held the keys to the pantry for fifty years announces she is going to run away with a travelling oil merchant. She is ninety. The merchant is seventy-four and has a bad knee. The household is paralysed. The aunt is packing.

choices.text: Give her your blessing, and a cart

effects.log: You give her your blessing and a cart. She leaves at dawn, humming, and sends a letter a year, always about the oil.

choices.text: Ask the merchant to come and live in the house

effects.log: You ask. The merchant moves in, with his knee, and the pantry has never been so well supplied.

events.text: The skiff of {b3_clan}, a large and useless thing, has sat in the shed for sixty years. A boy asks if he can fix it. You say yes, expecting nothing. Three months later he rolls it into the courtyard, humming, and offers you a ride.

choices.text: Take the ride

effects.log: You take it. It handles like a drunken ox and gets you across the lake in under an hour, and the boy is hired as the house's mechanic on the spot.

choices.text: Ask him to teach the other children how it was done

effects.log: You ask. He does, with sketches, and the house acquires a school of small inventors, none of them useful.

events.text: The house of {b3_clan} has a taboo: no one may speak of the Third Courtyard. It is a perfectly ordinary courtyard. No one remembers why. A visiting guest, asked politely not to mention it, mentions it at once. The room turns to stone. {b3_elder} slowly puts down a cup.

choices.text: Ask {b3_elder} to tell what is known of it

effects.log: {b3_elder} tells it: a quarrel, three centuries gone, a vow of silence made over one dead child. No one has dared break it, and no one has dared keep it.

choices.text: Propose to lift the taboo with a feast in the courtyard

effects.log: You propose a feast. It is held, grimly, and ends in an hour of laughing and weeping, and the courtyard is again just a courtyard.

events.text: A hawk has made its nest on the roof of {b3_clan}, and the servants are afraid of it. It has already carried off a hat, a duster, and the steward's wig. The hawk seems to like the house. {b3_peer} is for shooting it. A child is for naming it. The child names it Governor.

choices.text: Let Governor stay

effects.log: You let him stay. He steals the steward's wig seasonally, and the whole house watches it fly, and the steward has stopped objecting.

choices.text: Build Governor a proper perch above the gate

effects.log: You build the perch. Governor takes up residence, and will not allow any other bird in the courtyard, and the house is, for once, quiet in the mornings.

events.text: A traveller offers {b3_clan} a map of the unknown: a scroll, half burned, drawn by a lost expedition. The traveller wants a large sum and a home. The map is almost certainly a forgery. It is also, {b3_elder} points out, an extraordinary piece of work.

choices.text: Buy the map and give the traveller a room

effects.log: You buy the map and the room. The traveller turns out to be a gifted copyist and teaches the house to draw, and the map is hung above the stairs.

choices.text: Offer the traveller a room and no sum

effects.log: You offer the room alone. The traveller is offended for a day, and stays for ten years, and does not ever mention the map again.

events.text: At the funeral of the senior aunt of {b3_clan}, the mourning is interrupted by a stranger who walks into the hall and kneels at the coffin. He says he was her friend, for forty years, in letters, and never met her. The house has never heard of him. He has her letters in a satchel.

choices.text: Let him read one aloud

effects.log: He reads. It is witty, tender, and entirely unlike anything the house knew of her, and the hall, by the end, is laughing through tears.

choices.text: Receive the letters and keep them in the archive

effects.log: You receive them. The archive gains a whole second life of an aunt the house barely knew, and the stranger is given a seat for the rest of the funeral.

events.text: The wine-steward of {b3_clan} brings word that the great cask, laid down at the founding, is to be opened for the first time on the anniversary. It is not clear what is in it. The founder's will says "to be drunk by the one who most needs it." The house watches you with scarcely concealed greed.

choices.text: Take the first cup yourself

effects.log: You take it. It is rough and sweet and tastes of apples and an old kitchen, and you needed it more than you knew.

choices.text: Give the first cup to the oldest servant of the house

effects.log: You give it. The servant drinks, closes both eyes, and says it is the taste of a winter morning sixty years ago, and the hall is very quiet.

events.text: Your house has been invited to a debate among the great houses, on the topic "Is memory a duty?" The champion of {b3_clan} has fallen ill. {b3_peer} suggests the head step in. The opposition is a famously cruel logician from a house older than yours.

choices.text: Take the stand, and argue the question

ok.log: You argue that memory is a gift whose duty is to be handed on, and the logician has no reply, and the hall rises.

fail.log: You stumble in the second round, and the logician is courteous in a way that is worse than cruelty.

choices.text: Send a written argument and stay home

effects.log: You send an argument, three pages, plain. It is read aloud, and the logician replies in twenty, and the house is thought, if not victorious, at least sincere.

events.text: A servant of {b3_clan} is accused by the cook of stealing a ladle. The servant weeps and swears innocence. The ladle is found in the cook's own sleeve. Both are mortified. The servant, still weeping, says the cook is the kindest person in the house and must have had a reason.

choices.text: Ask the cook the reason

effects.log: The cook admits: the ladle was for a neighbour's dying wife, who loved the soup. You send the ladle, and a pot, and a servant to carry it.

choices.text: Say nothing and replace the ladle with a better one

effects.log: You replace it. The cook says nothing for a month, then turns up each morning with a bowl of the soup, placed silently at your door.

events.text: Dark rumours: someone in {b3_clan} is selling the house's secrets. {b3_peer} suggests a trap, a false document left on a desk. {b3_elder} says that was how the last head was ruined. The leak is real; three of the house's dealings have been undermined this season.

choices.text: Plant the false document, and watch

effects.log: You plant it. The leaker is, at the end of the week, revealed to be a very junior clerk who was simply lonely and wanted to be talked to by a rival envoy.

choices.text: Announce that you know, and give the leaker a week to come forward

effects.log: You announce it. On the sixth day the clerk comes forward, white as chalk, and the house keeps the clerk and moves them to a better table.

events.text: The great gate of {b3_clan} is to be repainted for the hundredth time. A committee has formed. It has been meeting for a year. It cannot decide between red and a different red. A child asks why not blue, and every adult in the room looks at the child with something close to fear.

choices.text: Paint it blue

effects.log: You paint it blue. The first week, half the house looks the other way. By the third month the neighbours are painting theirs.

choices.text: Dissolve the committee and let the child pick

effects.log: You dissolve it. The child picks green, and nobody dares object, and the gate is the most beloved thing in the district.

events.text: A pilgrim stops at {b3_clan} for a night and asks to see the ancestral tablets. The pilgrim stands before each, bows, whispers. At the end the pilgrim bows to the empty space at the end of the row, where yours will go. "A good space," says the pilgrim. "It is warm already."

choices.text: Ask the pilgrim what that means

effects.log: The pilgrim smiles and refuses to say. You think about it for years, and are never sure it was a blessing.

choices.text: Offer the pilgrim a night's rest and a good breakfast

effects.log: You do. The pilgrim leaves at dawn without a word, and a bowl of rice is left on the empty space, and nobody admits it.

events.text: Your steward reports that an outer wall of {b3_clan} has been, over the past year, very slowly moved outward, a hand's breadth at a time, by an unseen hand. The wall now encloses an extra courtyard and a small shed. Nothing has been taken. The shed contains a very old, very quiet kettle.

choices.text: Leave the shed, and let the wall be

effects.log: You leave it. The kettle is warm each morning, though nobody lights it, and the house drinks from it with a faint awe.

choices.text: Investigate the kettle

effects.log: You investigate. It is empty, ordinary, and boils at precisely the hour you were born, every day, and for no other reason.

events.text: A child of {b3_clan} falls ill, and a healer is sent for from a distant house. The healer arrives, examines the child, and says nothing can be done but wait. For nine days the whole household takes turns by the bed. On the tenth, the child sits up and asks for dumplings.

choices.text: Make the dumplings yourself

effects.log: You make them, badly. The child eats every one, and then laughs at the shape, and the house exhales for the first time in nine days.

choices.text: Send the healer a handsome gift

effects.log: You send it. The healer, delighted, sends back a letter with a recipe for the dumplings, which you try, and which is better.

events.text: An old rival of your late predecessor comes to {b3_clan} and asks, politely, to see the former head's study. The rival stands in it for an hour, touching books. At the end the rival says that they spent forty years hating that person, and that it was the great love of their life.

choices.text: Give the rival a book from the study

effects.log: You give them one. They hold it with both hands, and go away, and the book is returned to the house on the rival's death, with a note.

choices.text: Offer the rival tea in the study, and listen

effects.log: You listen. The rival talks until dark, and the study, which had been a room of absence, is filled with a person for one evening.

events.text: The neighbouring house owes {b3_clan} a favour so old that nobody remembers the favour, only the owing. Their head turns up at your gate with a basket of persimmons and an expression of dread, and says it is time to settle. The persimmons are very good.

choices.text: Name an easy favour and eat a persimmon

effects.log: You ask for a letter of introduction. The head is so relieved that a friendship begins over fruit.

choices.text: Name the old favour and ask them to say what it was

effects.log: The head cannot, and nor can you, and you laugh until the fruit is gone, and the debt is declared void.

events.text: The neighbour's head returns to {b3_clan} and says the letter you asked for was used. A young cousin of theirs has gone far on it. The cousin now holds a post, and in gratitude, the post has been opened to a young person of yours. The offer is made in person, with a bow.

choices.text: Send {b3_peer}'s youngest to take the post

effects.log: You send them. Within a year the young one is writing home about people you have never met, and the neighbour's house and yours are practically family.

choices.text: Decline, and propose the post go to a deserving stranger

effects.log: You decline. The neighbour is moved, and the stranger, when chosen, writes you a very long letter of thanks.

events.text: The young one you sent has come home, grown, with news. The neighbouring house is in trouble: an old charge, a threatened seizure, and no friends at the Jade Court. Their head sits in your hall, aged, saying nothing. The young one stands behind the old head, pleading with their eyes.

choices.text: Stand surety for the neighbour before the court

effects.log: You stand surety. It costs you a season of standing and a hundred small favours, and the neighbour's house remains, and so, from that day, does the friendship.

choices.text: Send gifts and a letter, but keep clear of the case

effects.log: You keep clear. The neighbour's house survives by other means, and the young one comes home quieter, and is never the same.

events.text: Your steward finds a child asleep in the great hall of {b3_clan} every dawn, curled under the table, with no explanation. No child of the house is missing. The child will say only that the hall is "the quiet one." The cook has been feeding the child for a month.

choices.text: Ask the child to share the hall in the day too

effects.log: The child comes, wary, and is soon running the library cat. The child will not say where they came from, and you do not ask.

choices.text: Trace the child's parents

effects.log: You trace them. They are in a house three streets away and had no idea. They come, mortified, and the child is returned with a new, quieter loyalty to the hall.

events.text: The ambassador of a distant house arrives at {b3_clan} for the winter, and the house does its best. On the third night the ambassador is found in the library weeping over a book of recipes. It is the ambassador's mother's hand. The book was, it seems, sold by a servant long ago.

choices.text: Return the book to the ambassador

effects.log: You return it. The ambassador kisses the cover, and promises the favour of a house you have never met, and means it.

choices.text: Offer to copy the book, and keep the original

effects.log: You copy. The ambassador takes the copy, and the original stays, and both are wary of each other for a season, and then not.

events.text: The women of {b3_clan} come to you as a body, nine of them, in their best, and say the house has too many rules about who may sit where. They have drawn a map. It is beautiful, and furious, and shows the dining hall with all seats marked in red. They want it changed.

choices.text: Redraw the seating, with their map

effects.log: You redraw. The first dinner is chaos and a joy, and the house looks different by dessert.

choices.text: Ask them to defend each red mark in turn

effects.log: You ask. They defend all forty-two, brilliantly, and you concede thirty-eight and keep four, which is, all agree, a masterpiece of diplomacy.

events.text: A pest has taken to the orchard of {b3_clan}: a kind of moth that eats fruit from the inside and leaves a perfect skin. The head gardener is distraught. The skins are all there, shining. Nobody knows until they bite. A guest bit one at lunch and has not been the same.

choices.text: Burn the infested trees and replant

effects.log: You burn them. The orchard is bare for three years, and the gardener takes it as a bereavement, and the new trees, when they come, are from seed carried across the sea.

choices.text: Invite a hundred birds with seed and let them work

effects.log: You do. The birds clear the moths in a season, and the house wakes each dawn to a riot of song, and the guest is quite recovered.

events.text: In {b3_clan}, the door to the old nursery has been locked for sixty years. No one remembers why. A small boy has found a key in a pocket of the old curtain. The whole family stands in the corridor, and nobody wants to be the one to say "open it."

choices.text: Open it yourself, in front of everyone

effects.log: You open it. The nursery is dust and toys and a small chair, and on the chair a faded drawing of the house, with every window lit, which makes the elders go very still.

choices.text: Send the boy in alone and wait at the door

effects.log: The boy goes. He comes out after a minute, holding a wooden horse, and says only that it was "very quiet and very kind."

events.text: A famous swordsman, grown old, asks to retire to {b3_clan} for the last of his days. He wants a cottage, a garden, and no questions. He has, you can tell, a great many enemies. The garden is nearly finished when the first of them arrives at the gate, politely, with a gift.

choices.text: Receive the visitor and set the terms

effects.log: You receive them in the hall, with tea. The visitor wants only to see the old man once, to say a thing. The swordsman, when told, comes out, and they sit in the garden until dark.

choices.text: Turn the visitor away at the gate

effects.log: You turn them away, courteously. The old swordsman never knows. He tends his garden for eleven years and dies among the beans.

events.text: The house of {b3_clan} has a festival in which the youngest child leads the procession through the gate with a lamp. This year the youngest is a boy of three who will not walk, will not be carried, and will not give up the lamp. The procession is waiting. The sun is going down.

choices.text: Carry the boy and the lamp yourself

effects.log: You carry him, lamp and all, at the head of the procession. He falls asleep on your shoulder, lamp lit, and the house walks behind in a hush, as in a dream.

choices.text: Let the boy sit where he is and bring the procession to him

effects.log: You bring the procession to him. It circles the lamp three times and the festival, which has never been done so, is declared the best in memory.

events.text: An ink-stone of great age is discovered in the wall of {b3_clan} while a mason is repairing a pillar. It is cracked, black, and warm. When wet, it produces ink of a faint blue, which dries clear. The only writing that stays is a note, in a hand nobody knows, that reads: "Do not let them forget the doors."

choices.text: Ask the scribes what doors are meant

effects.log: The scribes search for a month. They find an old plan of the house with eleven doors, and three have been bricked up. You open them.

choices.text: Keep the ink-stone in the archive and say nothing

effects.log: You keep it. It is warm each winter. Once, in the third year, you find a fresh line on the paper, in the same hand, saying: "Thank you."

events.text: A young heir of a great house, sent to {b3_clan} for the season as a guest, does nothing but sleep. For six weeks. The boy wakes at noon, eats, and sleeps again. {b3_elder} is irate. The boy's parents have sent word: do not wake him. He is, it turns out, recovering from something nobody will name.

choices.text: Let him sleep, and keep the house quiet

effects.log: You quieten the house. At the end of the season the boy wakes, bright-eyed, thanks everyone by name, and goes home, and his family remembers.

choices.text: Bring him gently into the daily life of the house

effects.log: You bring him in. By the end of the season he laughs at breakfast, and his parents write that they had given up hoping.

events.text: The scholars of {b3_clan} are in dispute over how to read a line in the founding charter. One reading says the house must always keep a guest-room open. The other says it must always keep a guest. Both are plausible. The difference, in practice, is one very odd permanent resident.

choices.text: Adopt the second reading and invite a permanent guest

effects.log: You invite one. A bookish old scholar accepts, and for forty years the house has a resident philosopher who corrects its grammar.
