choices.text: Adopt the first, and keep a room, with the bed made, always

effects.log: You keep it. The bed is made every morning for nobody, and once in a hundred years someone arrives who needed it.

events.text: A band of players arrives at {b3_clan} and offers a performance in exchange for a roof. The house is in a miserly mood. {b3_peer} points out that last time the house refused players, a curse followed. {b3_elder} says there was no curse; there was merely a very bad harvest.

choices.text: Take them in and give them the hall

effects.log: You take them in. They play for three nights, and the house, which had been sullen, is filled with an unfamiliar warmth.

choices.text: Give them the barn and a fair price

effects.log: You give them the barn. The players are content, the house is half-pleased, and the show is a success, but a distant one.

events.text: The children of {b3_clan} have been telling each other that there is a ghost in the cistern. It is a cistern. Nobody has ever seen a ghost in it. One child dares another, and the dared goes down on a rope and does not come up. The house runs to the rim with lamps.

choices.text: Go down yourself on the rope

effects.log: You go down. The child is at the bottom, delighted, with a frog in each hand. There is, you notice, a small arched door in the wall, and the child says "that is where the ghost lives."

choices.text: Direct the rescue from the rim

effects.log: You direct it. The child is brought up in a basket, smug, and the cistern is covered, and the arched door is never discussed.

events.text: A sudden snow falls on {b3_clan} in the wrong month, and the pear trees are all in blossom. The white lies across the white. A cart-driver at the gate cries that it is an omen. The house is divided between delighted and alarmed, and a child makes a snow pear that looks exactly like you.

choices.text: Close the gates and have a snow-day

effects.log: You close the gates. Everyone plays in the snow, and a snow pear is added to every doorstep, and the omen is whatever people decide.

choices.text: Send servants to knock snow off the trees before the blossoms freeze

effects.log: You send them. Half the blossoms are saved, and the harvest, in autumn, is a fruit pear that tastes faintly of cold.

events.text: The lawyer of {b3_clan} warns that a dying relative in a distant province has named the house in a will. The will has a clause: the heir must live a year in the relative's village. The relative was the least pleasant person in the family. {b3_peer} suggests refusing. {b3_elder} says the village has a very good river.

choices.text: Send a trusted cousin to live the year

effects.log: You send the cousin. A year later they return, tanned and calm, with a cat, a field, and a letter of thanks from the village.

choices.text: Go yourself for a season, and return

effects.log: You go. The village is kinder than the relative, and the river is as good as rumoured, and you come back lighter for it.

events.text: A famous beauty comes to {b3_clan} for a month and, by the end, half the household is in love with her. The other half is in love with her tutor. {b3_peer} says it is a plague. {b3_elder}, sighing, says it is spring.

choices.text: Hold a feast, and let the sentiments run their course

effects.log: You hold the feast. A dozen declarations are made, and two are accepted, and the house settles back with the ease of a pond after a stone.

choices.text: Quietly arrange for the beauty to leave early

effects.log: You arrange it. She goes, amused, with a note: "You are the sensible one. How dull." You keep the note.

events.text: Your cousin has decided to become a hermit, and has built a hut on the roof of the east gate of {b3_clan}. It is eight feet by six. He has been up there for a week. He says he has attained a kind of peace, and also that he is hungry, and also that the stairs are, after all, very far.

choices.text: Send a servant with food, and check on him daily

effects.log: You do. In a month he comes down, serene and thin, and says the roof has been the making of him, and goes back up on weekends.

choices.text: Tell him the roof is leaking and he had better come down for the rain

effects.log: You tell him. It does not rain for six weeks. He eventually comes down, looking suspicious.

events.text: The treasurer of {b3_clan} is so honest that nobody trusts him. He reports the smallest discrepancy at once. He weeps at overpayments. The house is on the verge of dismissing him on the sole ground that he makes everyone feel worse. {b3_elder} says an honest man is a rare treasure and also a great burden.

choices.text: Keep him, and send him on a long tour of the estates

effects.log: You keep him. On the tour he is received with trembling awe by every tenant, and returns with a ledger entirely in order and a new, shy confidence.

choices.text: Reassure him in private that the house values him

effects.log: You do. He bursts into tears, thanks you at length, and is a little less careful about small things thereafter.

events.text: A famed physician passes through the town of {b3_clan} and agrees to see the elders of the house. The physician finds nothing wrong with any of them, and says so, and charges a very high fee for the news. {b3_elder} is outraged. {b3_peer} points out that not being ill is worth a good deal.

choices.text: Pay the fee with a grin

effects.log: You pay. The elders are pleased in a grudging way, and the physician is offered a seat, and tells stories of other houses until the lamps are burned.

choices.text: Haggle, and win a smaller fee and a small lesson in diet

effects.log: You haggle. The physician is delighted by the sport and gives a lecture on porridge that the whole house follows for a year.

events.text: The boundary wall of {b3_clan} was built by a mason who left a single brick unmortared and a message in the old tongue: "Take me out when you are ready." The house has debated it for four hundred years. This year a very small girl, passing, takes the brick out and finds a smaller brick inside it, with a message.

choices.text: Read the message together as a house

effects.log: You read it. It says only: "You were always ready." The house is quiet for a moment and then, for no reason, applauds.

choices.text: Ask the girl to read it aloud first

effects.log: The girl reads it, in a loud, clear voice, and the elders hold their breath, and then, hearing it, begin to laugh, softly, with relief.

events.text: Every hundred years the well in the courtyard of {b3_clan} fills with a pale blue water that heals small wounds and bad tempers. It is the hundredth year. The house, which has never organised an event in its life, is preparing a ceremony. The well-keeper has appointed a committee of eight.

choices.text: Take the committee in hand and keep the ceremony small

effects.log: You keep it small. Everyone drinks, and the house is mild and pleasant for a week, and the well returns to plain water, and the committee is dissolved.

choices.text: Open the gates and let the whole district drink

effects.log: You open the gates. A thousand come, and the district is mild for a week, and the house is spoken of as generous, and the well-keeper weeps with joy.

events.text: The children of {b3_clan} stage a play for the household: "The Head and the Dragon." The head is played by a small boy in a robe three sizes too big, who gives a speech so like yours that the room freezes. The dragon, played by a cousin, is eaten by a spoon. At the end the boy bows, to you, and waits.

choices.text: Stand and applaud, loudly

effects.log: You stand and applaud. The room, released, applauds with you, and the boy turns scarlet and delighted, and is called "Head" by his cousins for a year.

choices.text: Rise and take the robe, and wear it for the rest of the evening

effects.log: You wear it. It trails the floor. The hall roars, and for one evening the head and the dragon are equally absurd, and equally loved.

events.text: Winter has been long, and the stores of {b3_clan} run low. {b3_peer} suggests dismissing eleven servants. The eleven are the oldest, the least useful, and the most loved. {b3_elder} says the house can survive a hungry spring, but not a cruelty. The ledger sits open between you.

choices.text: Keep everyone, and halve the head's own table

effects.log: You halve your table. The house sees. By spring, the lean broth is shared down to the last child, and nobody leaves.

choices.text: Dismiss four, with a pension, and keep seven

effects.log: You dismiss four and pension them. It is a compromise that hurts everyone a little and no one fatally.

events.text: A group of students from the school the house supports comes to {b3_clan} to petition against a master they say is dull. The master is brilliant and dry. They say he has not changed a word of his lectures in forty years. They are quite right, and he is equally right that the words are good.

choices.text: Ask the master to revise the lectures with the students

effects.log: You ask. The master, offended, then intrigued, takes six students as co-authors, and the new lectures are, in time, famous.

choices.text: Ask the students to hear the old lectures once more, carefully

effects.log: You ask. They do. Three, to their surprise, are moved, and four remain unmoved, and the petition is withdrawn.

events.text: Before the autumn feast, the head chef of {b3_clan} announces a new dish: a cold soup in a bowl of ice, which must be eaten in the first thirty seconds. The house is wary. {b3_elder} has declared that no good ever came of cold soup. The first guests are already seated with their spoons raised.

choices.text: Taste it first, in front of the guests

effects.log: You taste. It is astonishing, a mouthful of the whole summer, and the table sighs, and the chef stands very straight.

choices.text: Order a hot version as well, to be safe

effects.log: You order both. The cold one is gone in a minute; the hot one is eaten out of politeness, and the chef, wounded, is mollified by the third helping.

events.text: The mother of {b3_clan}'s young heir arrives unannounced from a distant province, thin, tired, and carrying a basket of eggs. She has not seen her child in six years. The house had been told she was dead. She sits in the courtyard and does not ask for anything.

choices.text: Bring the heir out to meet her, with no one else present

effects.log: You bring the child. The mother and the child look at each other for a long time, and then the child sits down beside her, and neither says a word, and the eggs are left in the sun.

choices.text: Quietly investigate who reported her dead

effects.log: You investigate. It was a steward, long since dismissed, who was bribed by a rival. The truth, once found, rights the heir's place in the house.

events.text: The north wing of {b3_clan} is so cold that no one will sleep in it. Servants talk of a draught. {b3_elder} talks of a spirit. A carpenter stays a night, and comes out at dawn pale and says the cold is not a draught but a very large, very patient, silent animal curled around the wing. It is asleep.

choices.text: Leave the wing as it is, and close the door gently

effects.log: You close the door. The wing is cold ever after, and the house uses it for storing ice and not much else, and the animal, if it is one, sleeps on.

choices.text: Sit a night in the wing and talk to it

effects.log: You sit and talk. At dawn the cold lessens a little, by a degree, and the wing is slightly warmer each year thereafter.

events.text: A famous critic visits {b3_clan} and writes an account of it so scathing and funny that it is passed from house to house. The head is called "a person of exquisite mediocrity." The household is mortified. {b3_peer} suggests a duel of letters. {b3_elder} has already begun laughing in the corridor.

choices.text: Write the critic a note of thanks and enclose a basket of persimmons

effects.log: You write the note. The critic is so disarmed that the next account is a love letter, and the house is, by common consent, charming.

choices.text: Quote the review at the head of your own gate

effects.log: You quote it, in gilt. The district roars. The critic, hearing, comes in person, to apologise and to be painted in front of the gate, which they have, in the end, mildly improved.

events.text: The great screen of {b3_clan} shows a mountain in mist, painted by a founder. A cousin, dusting, notices a figure in the mist that was not there last year. A tiny walker, on the path. By the next week the walker has climbed a hand-span. The house crowds round the screen with lamps.

choices.text: Mark the walker's place each day with a pin

effects.log: You mark it daily. The walker moves at a steady, unhurried pace. The house begins to guess aloud where it will stop.

choices.text: Cover the screen with a cloth

effects.log: You cover it. The house is divided, and servants peek, and in a month the cloth is found folded neatly, and the walker is nearer the top.

events.text: The little walker on the screen of {b3_clan} has reached a hut near the summit. A light has come on in the hut. The house falls silent every evening to watch the window. A child says someone in the hut is writing something. {b3_elder} says no one in the house is allowed to be that curious. Everyone is.

choices.text: Hang a lamp before the screen every night

effects.log: You hang a lamp. Every evening the window in the screen glows back, a little brighter, and the house falls into a habit of tenderness.

choices.text: Send a painter to copy the screen exactly

effects.log: You send one. The copy shows only a mountain in mist, and the painter, shaken, says the original has changed while being copied.

events.text: On the first day of spring the walker on the screen of {b3_clan} is gone, and the hut is empty, and the door open. The mountain is the same. But on the floor beneath the screen lies a folded paper, in the founder's hand, addressed to the head of the house. It is your name.

choices.text: Read it aloud to the house

effects.log: You read it. It is a short note of thanks for the lamp, and a blessing on the house, and a request that the screen be left uncovered ever after. The house obeys.

choices.text: Read it alone, and keep the contents to yourself

effects.log: You read it alone. It is warm, and personal, and you keep it in the lining of a sleeve for the rest of your life.

events.text: The singing master of {b3_clan} has a voice that cracks on the high notes, a fact the household has politely not noticed for thirty years. A visiting critic hears the master in the hall and says, aloud, to everyone, "that is the worst voice I have ever heard." The critic is asked to leave.

choices.text: Call the master to your study and ask for the song as it is meant

effects.log: The master sings it, cracks and all. It is the best performance of the song you have heard, and you say so, and you mean it.

choices.text: Pay the critic's fare and ask them never to return

effects.log: You pay. The critic goes. The master never learns of it, and sings as before.

events.text: The caretaker of the ancestral ground of {b3_clan} is found dead of old age in his sleep, and with him, the only complete map of the ground. The graves have no markers. The house has been burying its dead there for a thousand years. The grass is thick.

choices.text: Hold a quiet vigil, then walk the ground with every elder

effects.log: You walk it. Between them, the elders recall four hundred graves, and map them, and weep at the fifth hundred, which no one recalls.

choices.text: Raise a single great stone for all the unmarked dead

effects.log: You raise it. The stone is blank, and the house gathers before it each year, and the blank is, in time, taken to be full.

events.text: The household clerk of {b3_clan} finds that the house has, for generations, mislaid an entire hall. It is on the plans. It is not on the ground. A search is made. In a corner of the east wing, behind a wardrobe, is a door, and behind the door a hall, dusty, vast, and furnished.

choices.text: Open the lost hall and use it for the next feast

effects.log: You open it. The feast is the finest in memory, in a hall that smells of cedar and a century of waiting.

choices.text: Make the lost hall a quiet room for the old

effects.log: You make it a room for the old. They gather there each afternoon, and tell the oldest stories into the high shadows.

events.text: A fever runs through the lower town of {b3_clan}. The house's physician is overwhelmed. A poorer rival house, long hostile, sends its own healers without being asked. They arrive at dawn with baskets, say nothing, and begin to work. The head of the rival house stands at the gate in a cloak, not coming in.

choices.text: Go out to the gate, bareheaded, and thank the rival's head

effects.log: You go out. The rival's head, stiff, says it is nothing. You say it is not, and the head, for a moment, looks very old.

choices.text: Send out tea and a seat, and let the rival head decide

effects.log: You send them. The rival head sits at the gate for the whole day, drinking tea, watching their healers, and the feud, without a word, ends.

events.text: The gardener's apprentice at {b3_clan} has been replanting the old garden, row by row, according to no pattern. When the plants come up, they spell something in a script nobody knows. The head gardener, aghast, wants to rip them out. The apprentice says it is a sentence, and is very sorry, and doesn't know what it means either.

choices.text: Ask a scholar of old scripts to read it

effects.log: The scholar reads it with a long face: "Please water us." You water them. They flower, all at once, into a second sentence.

choices.text: Leave the plants and keep the gardener from touching them

effects.log: You leave them. They grow and fade, and in the autumn their seeds are caught in a net, and are planted elsewhere, and spell the same words.

events.text: A messenger from the Jade Court brings {b3_clan} a decree: the house must supply fifty men for a work-levy on a dam far away. The house has forty-one able men. The messenger has the patience of a stone. The decree is valid. The dam, {b3_peer} points out, is a very good dam.

choices.text: Supply fifty, borrowing nine from the neighbour house

effects.log: You supply fifty, with a loan of nine. They are returned in the spring, tanned and grave, with the dam in their eyes, and the neighbour house is owed a feast.

choices.text: Supply forty-one and plead the shortage

effects.log: You plead. The messenger records it with a careful face, and the shortfall is quietly forgiven, and noted in a file.

events.text: A raven has taken to carrying messages to {b3_clan} from an unknown sender: tiny notes in a shaky hand saying "the cellar," "the cellar," "the cellar." The house has searched the cellar six times. Tonight the raven stands on your desk and drops a tiny, rusted key.

choices.text: Take the key to the cellar yourself

effects.log: You go. Behind a barrel is a small iron door, and behind it a single shelf, with a single jar, labelled with your name and the year you were born.

choices.text: Send the key to the archive and ask for a comparison with old locks

effects.log: You send it. A match is found, in a drawer of a long-dead steward, and the lock turns out to belong to something else altogether.

events.text: The tenants of {b3_clan} ask for the privilege of building a small shrine at the edge of the estate. They have no particular deity in mind; they say they just want a place to put thanks. The shrine, when built, is a mound of stones, a bowl, and a very small bell. By midsummer it is covered in offerings.

choices.text: Visit the shrine on the first day of the harvest

effects.log: You visit. You leave a stone and ring the bell, and the tenants, watching from the fields, bow, and the harvest is the best in a decade.

choices.text: Declare the shrine under the protection of the house

effects.log: You declare it. A scribe writes it up, and the shrine is, in time, the busiest in the district, and no one gives credit to the house, which is the point.

events.text: A famed matchmaker arrives at {b3_clan}, unasked, carrying a list of seventeen candidates for a daughter of the house who is eleven. The matchmaker is not discouraged by her age. The daughter, listening at the door, comes in and asks what the criteria are. The matchmaker has never been asked.

choices.text: Let the daughter question the matchmaker

effects.log: She questions. By dusk the matchmaker has been politely reduced to a list of qualities, and the daughter has the first draft of a rulebook she will use at forty.

choices.text: Dismiss the matchmaker with a gift and a gentle warning

effects.log: You dismiss. The matchmaker leaves, amused, and the daughter, eavesdropping, runs to you with an expression of fierce gratitude.

events.text: The old watchtower of {b3_clan} has been crumbling for years, and the council wants it down. A boy has been sleeping in it. He says the tower talks, in the evenings, in a low, slow voice, about the weather of a century ago. He has a notebook full of it. The notes, you find, are correct.

choices.text: Keep the tower and give the boy the notebook and a stipend

effects.log: You keep it. The boy becomes the district's weather-sage, and the tower, buttressed, stands another hundred years.

choices.text: Let the tower come down, but save the notebook

effects.log: You let it fall. The boy cries, then sets about to teach himself to talk to wind in general, and does, quite well.

events.text: A new tutor at {b3_clan} teaches the children to argue both sides of every question, and the house erupts in debate. The cook argues against the menu. The gardener argues against the weather. {b3_elder} argues against the whole business, loudly, with great skill, and is awarded a prize by the children.

choices.text: Join a debate on the question "Is the head necessary?"

effects.log: You join, and argue the negative, and lose to a girl of nine. The house roars. You are made the Honorary Cause, and the girl goes far.

choices.text: Quietly award the tutor a raise

effects.log: You do. The tutor, shocked, writes back a formal letter of acceptance in three languages and a hundred and twelve words of rhetoric.

events.text: A merchant caravan stops at the gate of {b3_clan} in a storm. They carry silk, spices, and a sick child. The house takes them in. In the morning the child is well, and the merchant, deeply moved, offers a fraction of everything he carries. The house refuses, but the child will not let go of your sleeve.

choices.text: Accept a single bolt of silk, to be fair to the merchant's pride

effects.log: You accept one. The merchant bows deeply, and every year thereafter, on the same night, the caravan stops at your gate.

choices.text: Accept nothing, and ask only for news of the road

effects.log: You accept nothing. The merchant gives you news of a dozen provinces instead, and it proves more useful than silk.

events.text: A quarrel between the cooks of {b3_clan} has grown into a feud. There are two kitchens, in effect, eating different foods in the same dining hall. The head of the house is always served from both, to avoid offence, and has begun to resemble a pumpkin. Both cooks insist the other is poisoning the broth.

choices.text: Make both cooks taste each other's broth, blindfolded

effects.log: You blindfold them. Each pronounces the other's the better, and weeps, and the kitchens are merged.

choices.text: Declare a day of fasting for the whole house

effects.log: You declare it. The next morning both cooks are at your door, contrite, with baskets, and a new menu for the week.

events.text: An ancient oak at the gate of {b3_clan} is struck by lightning on a clear night. It splits in half and burns, and in the morning only the stump remains, and in the stump, a hollow, and in the hollow, a sleeping fox, unburned. The fox opens one eye. The household stands about it in a silent ring.

choices.text: Let the fox stay in the stump

effects.log: The fox stays. It is on the stump each morning, and by spring a plain white mark has appeared on its back where the lightning kissed it.

choices.text: Build a small roof over the stump, and a bowl

effects.log: You build the roof and the bowl. The fox accepts both, and presently several others come.

events.text: The head cook of {b3_clan} dies, and the funeral feast is cooked by her three apprentices, each in a different way. None of the dishes is the same. None of them is hers. The house eats in silence. Then the youngest apprentice brings out a plain bowl of rice, with a single pickled plum. The whole table puts down its chopsticks.

choices.text: Eat the plain rice first, and pass the bowl

effects.log: You eat first and pass it down the table. The rice is exactly as she made it, and every person at the feast is, for a moment, a child.

choices.text: Make the youngest apprentice the new head cook, then and there

effects.log: You name her. She nearly drops the bowl, and the table applauds with the grace of a family that has understood something.

events.text: A child of {b3_clan} discovers a way to climb to the roof from the library, behind a shelf. The child shows the cousins, and soon half the house is on the roof, watching the sunset. The steward, aghast, wants the passage sealed. The elder children are for keeping it. The younger have formed a guild.

choices.text: Install a rail, and keep the passage

effects.log: You do. The roof becomes the evening place of the house, and a thousand sunsets are shared, and the steward grows reconciled and, on one occasion, joins.

choices.text: Seal the passage and build a proper stair

effects.log: You build a stair. It is wider and safer and no one climbs it, and the guild moves its meetings to the library, behind the shelf.

events.text: A traveller who gave a lecture in {b3_clan} left behind a coat. In the pocket is a small leather book, closely written in a language no one can read, and a drawing of the house as seen from the sky. It is quite accurate. It shows a courtyard that was only dug last month.

choices.text: Send the book to a scholar of far tongues

effects.log: The scholar returns it in a season with a translation: a traveller's diary, and the last entry: "They are kind. I will come again, I think, in forty years."

choices.text: Keep the book in the study and wait for the traveller's return

effects.log: You keep it. Forty years on, a grey-haired traveller knocks at the gate and asks, with a bow, whether anyone has seen a coat.

events.text: A hungry beggar sits at the gate of {b3_clan} every day for a year, and never asks for anything. The servants have grown fond of him. The house gives him a bowl at noon. One day he is gone, and the bowl, left behind, has been scrubbed and filled with white pebbles, and arranged in the shape of the house.

choices.text: Keep the bowl on the hall shelf

effects.log: You keep it. A guest, years later, identifies the arrangement as a very old blessing. You do not tell the servants. They already know.

choices.text: Send servants to look for the beggar

effects.log: You send them. They find nothing, but they find, in the market, a rumour of a man who gives away pebbles, and who is said to be very happy.

events.text: An old story in {b3_clan} says that the house is built on the back of a sleeping turtle. Nobody believes it. This year the pond in the middle court begins to ripple at night, rhythmically, as with slow breathing. The cook claims her soup has begun to taste of salt. A child says the turtle is dreaming.

choices.text: Listen to the pond at night

effects.log: You listen. The ripples come in slow time, and under them a sound like a very distant song. You do not tell anyone, and you sleep better than you have in years.

choices.text: Have the pond measured and the ripples charted

effects.log: You chart them. They follow no pattern but one: the ripples quicken whenever the house is happy, and slow whenever it quarrels.

events.text: The house you serve sends you to buy a certain kind of ink. The seller says it is only sold to those who can say the name of the founder's dog. No one in {b3_house} knows it. On the way home, you stop at the grave of an old retainer and find, carved on the stone, a drawing of a small dog, and a name.

choices.text: Go back and say the name

effects.log: You say it. The seller weeps and sells you the ink, and a second jar, free, for the house.

choices.text: Tell the house about the stone and let them go themselves

effects.log: You tell them. The house sends a cart, and a sack of dog biscuits, and the ink is bought and the stone is cleaned.

events.text: {npc} has no wish to marry. {He} says so at once, over the first cup of tea, quite pleasantly. {He} has agreed to the meeting to please an aunt. {He} proposes that the two of you spend the afternoon being pleasant in public and then let the matter lapse. It is, you find, a very good plan.

choices.text: Agree, and make the afternoon as pleasant as possible

effects.log: You agree. The afternoon is so pleasant that at the end neither of you wants it to lapse, and the aunt, observing, orders more tea.

choices.text: Say you have no wish to marry either, and propose an alliance of friends

effects.log: You propose it. {npc} claps once, delighted, and the friendship lasts a very long time.

events.text: A cousin of {b3_clan} wants to marry a person nobody has met, from a village nobody has heard of, whom the cousin writes to every week. The letters are good. The cousin is radiant. {b3_elder} says it is a fraud. {b3_peer} says it is love. You have one letter to read, and it is long.

choices.text: Read the letter, and then write to the village yourself

effects.log: You write. The reply is very odd and very kind, and in a year the person arrives with a small dog and a large trunk, and is welcome.

choices.text: Send {b3_peer} to the village to see

effects.log: You send {b3_peer}. The report comes back in a month, glowing, and {b3_peer} returns with a basket of the village's peaches.

events.text: The scholars of {b3_clan} announce that a new star has appeared in the east, and that it is "very likely a comet." The cook announces that it is a sign. The old gardener says it is a lamp, and someone is looking for something. The star shines for nine nights and then vanishes. On the tenth, a stranger knocks.

choices.text: Admit the stranger and ask what is lost

effects.log: The stranger says: a way home. You give directions, bread, and a map. The stranger bows, and leaves at dawn, and the star does not return.

choices.text: Turn the stranger away until daylight

effects.log: You turn them away. At dawn the stranger is gone, and the doorstep holds a small silver coin, which shines at night.

events.text: The youngest children of {b3_clan} are all learning to read from one old primer, which has a rhyme on every page. Over the years the rhymes have been changed by the children, and the primer has grown. It is now a vast, strange, filthy document. {b3_elder} insists the original be restored. The children have mutinied.

choices.text: Let the primer stand as it is, and add your own rhyme

effects.log: You add one. It is read aloud at the next feast, and the whole house is in stitches, and the primer is bound in leather.

choices.text: Print the original and the children's version side by side

effects.log: You print both. The two volumes are inseparable, and used in schools beyond the district, to the mild fury of {b3_elder}.

events.text: Visitors to {b3_clan} always remark on the garden path, which meanders in absurd loops. It is the product of a quarrel, three hundred years ago, between two cousins. The loser had to design the path. The path is a masterpiece of stubbornness. A landscape artist wants to straighten it.

choices.text: Refuse, and add a plaque telling the story

effects.log: You refuse, and add the plaque. The path becomes a place of pilgrimage for people who believe in being wrong beautifully.

choices.text: Allow a single straightening, near the gate

effects.log: You allow it. The straight stretch is, within a year, the only part of the path anyone dislikes.

events.text: A messenger arrives at {b3_clan} in the dead of night with a letter from the dying head of a distant house. It names you as the guardian of their youngest daughter, whom you have never met. The girl, fourteen, is waiting at the gate with a bundle and the demeanour of a general at a lost battle.

choices.text: Welcome her as a daughter of the house

effects.log: You welcome her. She is silent for a month, and then she wins a debate against a visiting scholar, and her laughter is heard in the garden for the first time.

choices.text: Ask her what she wants, and arrange it

effects.log: You ask. She wants a library and a room with a lock. She gets both, and a seat at the table, and does not leave for thirty years.

events.text: The roof of the east pavilion at {b3_clan} has long been home to a colony of bats. Servants are afraid of them; guests are enchanted. A mason says they are damaging the beams. A scholar says they are eating the fruit pest. The council debates for a week. The bats, meanwhile, hold a vote of their own and move to the west pavilion.

choices.text: Let the bats settle in the west pavilion too

effects.log: You let them. The west pavilion is, within a year, the most atmospheric corner of the house, and a favourite with poets.

choices.text: Build the bats a proper house, with a small door

effects.log: You build it. The bats accept the house with an air of faint condescension, and the pavilions are restored.

events.text: A famous swordsman challenges {b3_clan} to produce a champion. The house has none. {b3_peer} suggests the gatekeeper, a stout old man with a limp. The gatekeeper accepts, with a worried frown, on the grounds that he has never lost a fight, having never had one. The duel is scheduled for dawn.

choices.text: Watch the duel from the wall

effects.log: You watch. The gatekeeper stands his ground with a broom, the swordsman, baffled, circles him for an hour, and withdraws with a bow, convinced the broom is a school of its own.

choices.text: Decline the challenge and offer the swordsman dinner

effects.log: You decline. The swordsman is not offended, and at dinner he teaches the gatekeeper a little, and the gatekeeper teaches him to cook.

events.text: The ancestral hall of {b3_clan} has a mirror in which, by tradition, the head looks at dawn on the first day of each year. It is ordinary, bronze, dim. You look. The face is yours, but older, and calm, and not in the least what you expected. It looks back, and nods once, and the mirror is simply a mirror again.

choices.text: Tell no one what you saw

effects.log: You tell no one. All year, you act as though you had been told something small and important, and the house, noticing, is curiously cheered.

choices.text: Ask the oldest servant what the head usually sees

effects.log: The servant, startled, says no one has ever said they saw anything. You both look at the mirror for a while.

events.text: The cooks of {b3_clan} receive a gift of a rare mushroom from a travelling trader. It is large, silver, and faintly luminous. The cooks are afraid to cook it. The trader says the mushroom must be eaten within the day. A guest at dinner volunteers, rashly, to taste a mouthful first.

choices.text: Let the guest taste, and watch closely

effects.log: The guest tastes, goes still, and says in a tiny voice that he can hear the soil breathing. He is fine by morning, and a changed man for a week.

choices.text: Decline the mushroom and plant it in the garden

effects.log: You plant it. By spring a ring of silver grows there, and children sit in it and tell each other very good lies.

events.text: Before a long journey, the head of a friendly house gives you a gift: a small wooden box of earth from their garden, to be scattered on your own when the time comes. They say it will make the two houses one soil. They do not say how long they expect the journey to last. {b3_elder} looks uneasy.

choices.text: Scatter the earth in your garden at once

effects.log: You scatter it. The two gardens bloom the same colours that spring, and a bond that had been ceremonial turns real.

choices.text: Keep the box until the head returns

effects.log: You keep it. The head returns after three years, thinner, and sees the box on your shelf, and sits down, unsteady, and says it was the thing that kept him going.

events.text: The children of {b3_clan} form a secret society, whose rules are too complicated for the members to follow. Its meetings are held in the attic. It has a flag, a handshake, and a treasury of seventeen buttons. They have petitioned the head for formal recognition. The petition is five pages, in crayon.

choices.text: Grant recognition, with one condition: a meeting minute in every month

effects.log: You grant it. The minutes are the most revealing record the house has ever had of itself, and you read them with an ache.

choices.text: Attend one meeting in disguise

effects.log: You attend. You are found out in a minute, and made a member on the spot, and sworn to secrecy, which you keep.

events.text: The longest-serving gatekeeper of {b3_clan} announces, quite calmly, that he is going to die on Thursday. He has put his affairs in order. He asks only that the house hold his wake on the Wednesday so that he may attend. The house is struck dumb. The doctor is called. The doctor finds nothing amiss.

choices.text: Hold the wake on Wednesday

effects.log: You hold it. He is at the head of the table, glowing, telling stories. On Thursday morning he is found asleep, content, and gone.

choices.text: Ask him how he knows

effects.log: He says: "The dog told me." The dog, a lean old terrier, lifts its head from the step and returns it, as if the matter were closed. On Thursday it is true.

events.text: A wandering poet, hired to entertain a feast at {b3_clan}, composes an ode to the house so full of flattery that the household is embarrassed. A few lines are insulting, if one reads them backwards. The poet, caught, explains that all flattery should be read backwards. He asks if he may stay.

choices.text: Make him the house poet, on a one-year trial

effects.log: You make him. He writes one honest line a month, and the house comes to look forward to it, and he stays for thirty years.

choices.text: Pay him in full and ask him to write the same ode for the neighbouring house

effects.log: You pay him. The neighbouring house, flattered, sends a gift, and later discovers the backwards reading, and sends another.

events.text: A servant has been dismissed from {b3_clan} for a trifling offence. At the gate she turns and says quietly that the house has been warm for years because of the third furnace, and that the furnace has a flaw, and that tonight it will go. She names no more, and walks into the dark. {b3_elder} says to ignore her.

choices.text: Check the furnace

effects.log: You check. It is cracked from end to end, and was a day from failing. The servant is found and offered her place back with an apology, and a raise she turns down with great dignity.

choices.text: Trust the servant and shut the furnace down

effects.log: You shut it down. At midnight there is a roar and a crack, and in the morning the house is cold, and very grateful.

events.text: The bridge at the edge of {b3_clan}'s land has no railing, and the village children play on it. A lad falls in and is fished out, spluttering. The lad's father demands a railing. The council argues the cost. The lad, wrapped in a blanket, announces that he has seen what is under the bridge and it is "a very big fish with a sad face."

choices.text: Build the railing, and put a bench by it

effects.log: You build both. The big sad fish is seen again by many, and the bench becomes the district's favourite place to sit and feel sorry for something.

choices.text: Build the railing, and ask the lad to draw the fish

effects.log: You build it and ask. The lad draws it, and it is, remarkably, a perfect portrait of the house's own steward, which the steward finds a deep honour.

events.text: A famous chess master, passing through, is challenged by a child of {b3_clan} to a game. The master, amused, accepts. The game lasts all night. By morning the master has been beaten in a way that bears no resemblance to any known opening. The child is asleep over the board. The master asks, shaken, who the child's tutor was.

choices.text: Say the child taught herself from a book of poems

effects.log: You say so. The master stares, then bursts out laughing, and offers the child a place in his own school. The child declines, firmly, for her cat.

choices.text: Say the child has no tutor, and let the master wonder

effects.log: You say nothing. The master leaves in a state of reverent unease, and the legend of the house, in chess circles, grows.

events.text: The lamps of {b3_clan} burn a strange colour tonight: a pale green, like new leaves. No one has changed the oil. The servants stand about, uneasy. The old watchman says that this has happened once before, in his grandfather's youth, and that the next day a child was born who could speak with rain.

choices.text: Wait through the night, and see

effects.log: You wait. At dawn a child is indeed born in the lower town, to a weaver and a potter, and the first words the child says are to the weather.

choices.text: Send for the midwives of the district, just in case

effects.log: You send. Three babies are born before noon, and the house is fond of all of them, and nobody can say which, if any, hears the rain.

events.text: The treasurer of {b3_clan}, who is also its best baker, has been secretly diverting flour from the granary to feed the poor of the lower town. The books show a modest, regular shortfall. The council demands a punishment. The treasurer stands, floury, hands folded, and says he will gladly accept any it chooses.

choices.text: Make the flour official, and double the amount

effects.log: You make it official. The lower town sends up a cake that same week, and the treasurer weeps into the dough.

choices.text: Let the matter pass, and quietly cover the shortfall

effects.log: You cover it. The treasurer, who knows, says nothing, but a loaf appears at your door every morning for the rest of his life.

events.text: An orphan boy brought into {b3_clan} as a kitchen helper turns out to be a gifted mathematician. He solves the steward's accounts in his head, finds errors in the ancestral calendar, and corrects a page of the founder's own sums. The cook is proud and terrified. The boy still washes the pots.

choices.text: Give him a tutor and a place in the study

effects.log: You give him one. At twenty he is the house's chief reckoner, and he still washes the pots, on Thursdays, as a sort of devotion.

choices.text: Send him to the academy at the house's expense

effects.log: You send him. He returns after nine years, famous, and builds a clock for the gate that keeps time to the second.

events.text: In the third year of a mild winter, a plague of snails attacks the vegetable gardens of {b3_clan}. The gardeners are in despair. A child suggests putting out saucers of beer. The gardeners are scandalised. The beer is put out. In the morning there are four hundred drunk snails and a very quiet garden.

choices.text: Carry the snails to the woods in baskets

effects.log: You carry them. It is the most ridiculous procession in the house's history, and the gardens flourish afterwards, and the snails send back no word.

choices.text: Let the snails sleep it off and tell the gardeners to learn from this

effects.log: You say so. The gardeners, humbled, adopt the beer, and become known as the best in three counties.

events.text: The roof of the library of {b3_clan} springs a leak, and the water drips on a rare scroll. The librarian, in tears, throws himself across the scroll. The scroll is saved, the librarian soaked. A carpenter is sent for. In the meantime the librarian refuses to leave the scroll, and sleeps with it, and is found at dawn in a state of delirious joy.

choices.text: Place a bucket, and bring the librarian a dry blanket

effects.log: You do. The scroll is moved to the safe, and the librarian is moved to the infirmary, and both recover.

choices.text: Commission a copy of the scroll before it is moved

effects.log: You commission a copy. The copy takes two years, and the scribe falls in love with the text, and writes a commentary.

events.text: A new maid at {b3_clan} has the odd habit of talking to the flowers. She does it quietly, and the gardeners, at first amused, have noticed that the flowers she talks to bloom a fortnight earlier. The head gardener asks her what she says. She says she asks them how they are. The gardener tries it.

choices.text: Make her an assistant gardener

effects.log: You make her one. The gardens of {b3_clan} are, within three years, the finest in the province, and she is paid more than the head gardener, who does not mind.

choices.text: Ask her to teach the whole household to ask

effects.log: She teaches them. The house becomes, for a while, a place where everyone asks everything how it is, and the effect is lasting and mild.

events.text: A kitchen boy is found to have been pocketing a spoonful of sugar every day for a year. His mother is ill and loves sweet tea. The steward, shocked, calls for the boy to be sent away in disgrace, which the house has not done since the founding. {b3_elder} looks at you. You are the head. You have a spoon in your hand.

choices.text: Give the boy a bag of sugar and a note for the mother

effects.log: You give him both. The boy bursts into tears and the whole kitchen is silent for a minute. The mother lives another nine years.

choices.text: Have the boy bring his mother to the house

effects.log: You send a cart. The mother is installed in a sunny room, with sweet tea, and the boy is made her keeper.

events.text: The wedding procession of a cousin of {b3_clan} crosses a market and meets a funeral procession going the other way. The street is narrow. Neither will give way. Both have brass bands. The two bands, locked nose to nose, begin to play at each other, louder and louder, until a goat runs through, and everyone laughs, and the street clears.

choices.text: Join the two processions and hold a single feast

effects.log: You join them. The feast is part wedding, part wake, and the weeping and the laughing are indistinguishable, and the family, afterward, are closer than before.

choices.text: Direct the funeral to pass first with honour

effects.log: You direct it. The wedding party stands in respect, and the bride, in red, weeps, and the whole market falls quiet, and the world is briefly just.

events.text: The boundary of {b3_clan} is walked every spring by a single servant with a stick, tapping each marker stone in turn. This year the servant taps one and it rings, hollow. Beneath it, in a hollow, is a tiny bronze bell, green with age, and a strip of paper with three characters nobody can read.

choices.text: Hang the bell above the gate

effects.log: You hang it. It rings once a year, on its own, in spring, and the servant says that is the bell talking to the stone.

choices.text: Send the paper to a scholar

effects.log: The scholar reads it in a month: "Do not forget the walking." The servant walks on, vindicated.
